description:
- three songs by single adult male.
- sound editing in Audacity consisted mostly of a high pass filter with a 6dB rolloff below 1000 Hz, and a low pass filter with a 6dB rolloff above 8000 Hz and subsequent amplification (no clipping allowed); any removal of extraneous noise done by silencing rather than cutting to preserve song interval.
- bird singing from atop an alder along south bank of the Nechako River. 
- immediate habitat is bottomland cottonwood forest with dense riparian growth of willows and alders.

- typical advertising song of Alder Flycatcher.
- recording device: H2 Zoom; microphone: Sennheiser ME-66 attached to H2 disabling its internal microphones. Clip is mono as a result even though the H2 still labels it as being stereo.
- recording available in WAV format upon email request.

title: XC319017 Alder Flycatcher (Empidonax alnorum)
location: Bangor, Penobscot County, Maine
description:
Recorded on iPhone 5 using EIM-001 microphone and RODE Rec app. Imported to Audacity with minor trim to shorten the gaps and eliminate "dead air". High Pass Filter to 2400Hz with a rolloff of 24dB to eliminate the nearby foot traffic noise.

Marsh environment. Bird was in a bush beside the small side marsh at this location. Was sitting and would occasionally hunt. Otherwise rather stationary. 

Noted that this bird made its call during the pauses between other birds calling in the vicinity. Other bird sounds were edited out for the purpose of making this call be at the foreground. In the original there was a gap of about 5-7 seconds between each of these calls in which other birds were singing.
author: rob.oconnell

Singing from trees adjacent to ponds. There is an interesting double-vocalization at 1:20.5, where either the bird stutters or a second individual sings nearby. Perhaps it is a Willow Flycatcher? Also, Willow Flycatcher at 0:05?

 Clear sky, about 60°F,  warming from an overnight freeze.

## Equipment

Recorded on a Sennheiser MKE 400 microphone with a wind baffle into a Panasonic GH2 camera at 192 kbps.

## Modifications

 Trimmed stretches without songs from front  and back. Amplified to peak at –3.0 dB.

location: Laguna Lake, San Luis Obispo County, California
description:
This American Bittern is likely the same individual as the one I recorded on 3-24-17 with my iPhone and iXY Rode microphone ( XC361329 ), but here I’m using my ME67 Sennheiser  shotgun microphone and PMD 661 Marantz recorder. I used some noise reduction, a high pass filter at 60 dB, and  normalized the volume, but I also reduced the length from a 30 minute recording, with lots of handling noise created as I slowly walked closer, to 3.5 minutes with about 15 seconds between each call. I overlapped each of the 10 calls, fading out and in to blend them.

This bird was in a marshy field, about 100 feet away from me.

description: We had heard another individual singing across the beach marshland less than 30 minutes previously, so this bird could be a female, its mate. Flight call as it flushed and flew away from me. Pretty startling, almost stepping on a completely camouflaged Bittern... Anyway, weather cool (~50 degrees F), no wind, overcast. Bird was only 2m away from me when we surprised each other, and I pounded "Record". Short earsplitting click from that was removed at beginning, though a small remnant remains in its first call. # Habitat #
State waterfowl refuge along the margins of USACE flood control reservoir. Strip along the lake margins ~1km wide of moist soil grassland with mix of forbs, native warm season grasses (Andropogon, Schyzachyrium, Eragrostis, Aristida, etc.), and some sparse woody vegetation (Cephalanthus, Quercus saplings, etc.) bounded by oak hickory forest and, in places, pine plantation.  Three or four shallow waterfowl impoundments partially flooded in the winter.

# Editing #
Adobe Audition. Butterworth high-pass filter, cutoff 1 khz, order 3.

# Equipment #
Fostex FR-2 digital field recorder with Telinga Pro 22" parabolic reflector

The call was a short high note but I am not sure if I recorded it, I don't find it ( I am afraid I mixed it with  the call of Luscinia svecica).

description:
American pipits recorded at the edge of a large meadow.  Two adults and one fledgling, so I'm assuming one adult was female and the other was male.  Also photographed.  The birds were only a few meters from me along a trail.  

The first few sounds are from the fledgling and then the adults start calling.  My voice is audible after a flurry of sounds from the adults.  

Equipment: Sony PCM-M10 recorder and a Sennheiser MKE-400 microphone. 
Modifications to the file: cropped at both ends.

This is another example of where it would be really helpful if XC used names adopted by the AOU for birds in North America.   The name used by XC is not well known on this continent.

title: XC315359 American Redstart (Setophaga ruticilla)
location: Oxford, Lafayette County, Mississippi
description:
Natural sound. Bird foraging in the lower branches of a Tulip Poplar on the edge of the grounds, 3-6m above the ground. Mostly moving along the branches picking from the leaves. Occasionally sallying to catch an insect in the air. 

#Habitat#
29-acre estate centrally located in Oxford, MS consisting of antebellum home surrounded by lawns and adjacent forest. Privet hedges and small thickets divide the grounds into distinct lawn units. Bordered on all sides by mature oak-hickory forest. Forest edge consists of oak spp, hickory spp, red cedar, mulberry, with understory along the edge dominated by privet (Ligustrum sp.). Grounds around the house include isolated trees and manicured hedges. A path from the end of the parking area leads northward ~1 km through the forest to the northern edge of the property abutting the University of Mississippi campus

#Editing#
Edited in Adobe Audition. Butterworth high-pass filter, order 3, cutoff frequency 800 Hz

#Equipment#
Fostex FR-2 digital recorder with Sennheiser microphone and Telinga pro 22" parabolic reflector.
background: Carolina Wren (Thryothorus ludovicianus); Wood Thrush (Hylocichla mustelina)
author: J.R. Rigby

title: XC309318 American Robin (Turdus migratorius)
location: Oxford, Lafayette County, Mississippi
description:
Natural sound. Bird singing from the lower branches of a large bare tree near the center of the grounds, surrounded by open lawns.  

#Habitat#
29-acre estate centrally located in Oxford, MS consisting of antebellum home surrounded by lawns and adjacent forest. Privet hedges and small thickets divide the grounds into distinct lawn units. Bordered on all sides by mature oak-hickory forest. Forest edge consists of oak spp, hickory spp, red cedar, mulberry, with understory along the edge dominated by privet (Ligustrum sp.). Grounds around the house include isolated trees and manicured hedges. A path from the end of the parking area leads northward ~1 km through the forest to the northern edge of the property abutting the University of Mississippi campus

#Editing#
Cut from a longer recording of ~4 min.

#Equipment#
Fostex FR-2 digital recorder with Sennheiser microphone and Telinga pro 22" parabolic reflector.
author: J.R. Rigby

The group is generally silent except for calls from 1 or 2 birds, except when small groups of other Wigeons arrive.  This recording includes calls during the separate arrivals of 4 groups of smaller numbers of Wigeons.  There are calls from some of the new arrivals, as they swim closer, and a chorus of calls from the established larger group. 

The recording is made at 9:30 p.m., more than 5 hours after 4:22 p.m. sunset.  The Wigeons are a resting in the ocean 1 to 5 meters from a sandy beach.  There are about a dozen Mallards resting on the beach.  There is a Great Blue Heron resting on a nearby rock but is not heard in this recording.

title: XC217766 American Woodcock (Scolopax minor)
location: Mount Vernon (near  Alexandria), Fairfax County, Virginia
description:
This recording was extracted from a video recorded on a Canon 7D mark II DSLR using the on-camera mic.  An FFT filter was used to affect an exponential roll-off in volume below 3 kHz to remove the sound of nearby George Washington Memorial Highway.   Adobe Audition's "adaptive noise removal" filter was then applied to get rid of background hiss.    One brief section of about 2 seconds in the middle of the video was removed in which a person in my group spoke.  The AMWO was in flight and distant at that point; no significant audio was lost.  

The recording was made while standing on the "dogleg" portion of the Haul Road trail at Dyke Marsh.  There were at least three male American Woodcocks in the area, and the one recorded here was within four meters while on the ground.  It was doing the standard AMWO breeding display which starts with a number of nasal "peent" calls followed (at 0:20) by a rapid vertical flight in which the tail feathers make a sound reminiscence of that made by Mourning Doves.   The bird reached an altitude of maybe 20 meters, then flew around in a wide circle, reaching its farthest point from me at about 0:42.   As the bird returned to its starting point above me at about 1:00, it began making the characteristic rapid chirp calls as it descended.  When it reaches the ground at 1:18, the bird goes totally silent.  The "peents" would start up a few seconds later and this cycle was repeated numerous times over the course of about 15 minutes.
background: Mallard (Anas platyrhynchos); Canada Goose (Branta canadensis)
author: Mouser Williams

title: XC127999 American Tree Sparrow (Spizelloides arborea)
secondary_labels: ['Cardinalis cardinalis_Northern Cardinal', 'Aix sponsa_Wood Duck', 'Turdus migratorius_American Robin', 'Poecile atricapillus_Black-capped Chickadee', 'Melospiza melodia_Song Sparrow', 'Anas platyrhynchos_Mallard', 'Branta canadensis_Canada Goose']
location: Richardson Nature Center, Hennepin, Minnesota
description:
Songs and calls from a wintering flock of 20-30 in a patch of scrub in oak savanna. This recording is comprised of several segments with slight breaks between them.  Most of the time, the birds were calling, singing, and chasing eachother around the bushes.  Occasionally small groups would make forays out into the grasses to forage, and then return.

At approximately 8:36, a Northern Shrike appears. There's an alarm call from one of the sparrows and they all stop singing and dive into the thickest part of the scrub.  Chickadees start scolding. There is some thrashing of wings as the shrike chases the birds (unsuccessfully) through the bushes, and all of the birds scatter.

Recorded from about 10m. Windy, cold, and overcast.  Filtered low frequencies slightly for wind, traffic, and airplane noise. Recorded with Olympus LS-10S and homemade parabolic reflector.
background: Northern Cardinal (Cardinalis cardinalis); Wood Duck (Aix sponsa); American Robin (Turdus migratorius); Black-capped Chickadee (Poecile atricapillus); Song Sparrow (Melospiza melodia); Mallard (Anas platyrhynchos); Canada Goose (Branta canadensis)
author: Jonathon Jongsma

title: XC153035 Anna's Hummingbird (Calypte anna)
location: Salem, Polk, Oregon
description:
Recording level was normalized, no filtering applied. Used equipment - Tascam DR-100 with unidirectional built-in microphone. Some echo could be caused by parallel walls surrounding the recording location.

Female was sitting in the middle of dense bush (2m from the ground) between two houses and producing series of clicking sounds. 

This female visiting my feeder, located in 9 feet (3m) from bush mentioned above, many times every day at least for one month before this record was made. This is the first time, when I've noticed such a behavior. Male of the same species was humming around while female was singing.

Photo were taken right before the recording: <http://www.flickr.com/photos/bushman_k/10600919896/>
author: Bushman

High pass filter was used to remove street noise below 1.8kHz

title: XC277243 Ash-throated Flycatcher (Myiarchus cinerascens)
location: Palo Verde, Imperial County, California
description: Sound amplified.  Habitat a sparse mix of mostly tamarisk and arrowweed with some mesquite and other desert vegetation.  The birds were in short vegetation (less than 2 meters off the ground) within a few meters of me.  This is an interaction between two ATFLs at a territory boundary.  They behaved aggressively towards each other, getting in to some fluttering squabbles.  Both birds were giving this call, but this recording is primarily of one individual.  The vocalizing bird is believed to be a female, as the male was detected nearby giving the territorial "Ka-breer!" call.  She had been carrying food all morning in to a mesquite about 50 meters west from where she is calling.  The nest was in this mesquite and now has at least 4 dependent young.  The agitated manner of the call and the aggressive behavior is the result of a member of a neighboring pair (believed to be the female as well) coming to the territory boundary within 50 meters of her young.  The second pair was observed multiple times carrying food in to a tamarisk about 75 meters SE of the spot this interaction took place.
author: Jennifer Tobin

title: XC428701 Barn Swallow (Hirundo rustica)
location: Inishbofin, Co. Galway
description: The clip is edited from several minutes of sounds made by two young Swallows that were sitting on a cottage roof. At least one parent was 'keeping an eye' on them and (probably) occasionally arriving to feed them.  I did not see any of the activity as I left the recorder and then played back the result. The opening ten seconds contain a burst of calls that accompanied the youngsters flying off [0:02]. This was when I left the recorder on the cottage roof, thereby disturbing them. At some point, a Wren landed on the roof and it must have perched right beside the recorder because its song is loud and clear at 0:10. After that, the Wren changes perch and the subsequent song-bursts are not so close. From 0:30, the young Swallows are resting on the roof and making typical twitters - the sound of offspring hoping to receive food from an incoming parent. It seems that, at around forty seconds, an adult flies in and may have delivered food - the calls become more intense at 0:45. Irrespective of whether the young were fed or not, they fly off at the end of the recording.
author: Anthony McGeehan

Natural sound. Foraging along the central branches of a large tree in a thin strip of forest between houses.

#Habitat#
29-acre estate centrally located in Oxford, MS consisting of antebellum home surrounded by lawns and adjacent forest. Privet hedges and small thickets divide the grounds into distinct lawn units. Bordered on all sides by mature oak-hickory forest. Forest edge consists of oak spp, hickory spp, red cedar, mulberry, with understory along the edge dominated by privet (Ligustrum sp.). Grounds around the house include isolated trees and manicured hedges. A path from the end of the parking area leads northward ~1 km through the forest to the northern edge of the property abutting the University of Mississippi campus

#Editing#
Adobe Audition. Butterworth high-pass filter, cutoff 1000 hz, order 3

#Equipment#
Fostex FR-2 digital recorder with Sennheiser microphone and Telinga pro 22" parabolic reflector.

title: XC265043 Belted Kingfisher (Megaceryle alcyon)
location: Eureka, Humboldt County, California
description:
This 6+ minute recording documents various sounds of two Belted Kingfishers. One was an adult female. The other was a juvenile female. I got the sense that the adult was forcing its offspring to leave home. This recording is poorly narrated thus many of the vocalizations are not identified to the individual. But on the upside, several are.

The first 10 seconds are several highlights of the recording mostly various juvenile vocalizations. But one adult noise as well.  

0:00 Begging of juvie while being chased by adult.

0:03 Expression of contempt followed by a rattle both juvie (not supremely confident that the rattle was juvie)

0:05 Two juvenile rattles.

0:08 Adult rattle.

0:30 The juvenile performed a display flight to meet and greet a 3rd BEKI. It was a juvenile and I suspect it was a sibling.

4:56 An interesting vocalization that I have a vague recollection that the juvie made. But I’m not certain.

More details of the context of this recording may be found here: <http://ebird.org/ebird/view/checklist?subID=S24410024>

This recording was made with an iPhone 5s with built-in microphone and Røde Rec application. This recording is largely an unedited and unmodified recording of the natural spacing of this bird's utterances. However, a 32 second period was removed starting at 1:56 due to a lull in the action. I also removed a 45 second period starting at 5:18 due to another lull. This recording is part of a longer 11 minute recording but due to a helicopter overflight and a brief spat between two nearby kayaker, I decided to leave it out.
background: Barn Swallow (Hirundo rustica); American Goldfinch (Spinus tristis)
author: Elias Aristides Elias

Natural sound. Bird disturbed by my approach, flew around the small pond and perched on an overhanging limb. Intermittently vocalizing and making short flights over the water.
 
#Habitat#
Small, tree-lined pond ~1acre. State waterfowl refuge along the margins of USACE flood control reservoir. Strip along the lake margins ~1km wide of moist soil grassland with mix of forbs, native warm season grasses (Andropogon, Schyzachyrium, Eragrostis, Aristida, etc.), and some sparse woody vegetation (Cephalanthus, Quercus saplings, etc.) bounded by oak hickory forest and, in places, pine plantation.  Three or four shallow waterfowl impoundments partially flooded in the winter.

#Editing#
No edits.

Fostex FR-2 digital recorder with Sennheiser microphone and Telinga pro 22" parabolic reflector.

title: XC225350 Bewick's Wren (Thryomanes bewickii)
location: Los Alamos, Los Alamos County, New Mexico
description:
This recording was extracted from a video I took with a Canon 7D Mk II DSLR.   I ran Adobe Audition's adaptive noise removal filter on it to cut down on white background noise.  

I could hear the bird singing at reasonably close range when I got out of my truck but couldn't see it.  I didn't recognize the song so I took a video to capture this audio.  It had been repeating this song pattern for about a minute by the time I got the video.   At 0:20 the bird switches to a repeated call note.  Looking for the bird caused it to go silent and presumably fly away without me seeing it.
author: Mouser Williams

title: XC215995 Black-billed Cuckoo (Coccyzus erythropthalmus)
location: Pequonnock watershead, Passic Co., NJ
description: Call in response to whistled imitation of song. Bird was about 2-4m up in hickory-chokecherry deciduous forest with some red maple mixed in on rocky ridgetop. Originally responded to a vocalizing C. americanus that had given the decelerating call, but also responded well to whistled imitation of song. Foraging on tent caterpillars while being observed. Edited below 1000 Hz to remove passing jet.
author: Dan Lane

title: XC215998 Black-billed Cuckoo (Coccyzus erythropthalmus)
secondary_labels: ['Setophaga discolor_Prairie Warbler', 'Passerina cyanea_Indigo Bunting', 'Baeolophus bicolor_Tufted Titmouse']
location: Pequonnock watershead, Passic Co., NJ
description: Call in response to whistled imitation of song. Bird (same as XC215995) in mixed deciduous woodland in on rocky ridgetop. The bird bombed in to the whistled imitation with a caterpillar in its bill, then saw us and flew back into the vegetation. These three vocalizations are not naturally spaced, as I removed dead air, voice annotations, etc., in between. Furthermore, the first vocalization has been 'doctored up' a bit by attaching the initial part of the third vocalization to it so it is 'complete'. The second vocalization was cut off because I turned on the cassette recorder after it began vocalizing.
background: Prairie Warbler (Setophaga discolor); Indigo Bunting (Passerina cyanea); Tufted Titmouse (Baeolophus bicolor)
author: Dan Lane

location: Olympia, Thurston County, Washington
description: Normalized to -3dB. 68°F, 5% cloud cover, light intermittent breeze from west. Residential setting on the edge of a greenbelt with Douglas fir and Bigleaf Maple dominant. From 0:00 to 0:42 a single bird perched 10' high in a small birch tree giving tseet calls while preening (feather ruffling audible). From the same location it then gave a series of chick-a-dee type calls beginning around 0:34.5. At 1:11 a second bird flew in and both quickly moved to a medium sized bush 25' away, at which point vocalizations changed to gargle call types (could not tell which bird), then a mix of both chick-a-dee and gargles. Two more birds landed 50' to the north and gave chick-a-dee calls. There were 4 birds total, however neither group of 2 came within 50' of each other.

title: XC375904 Black-headed Grosbeak (Pheucticus melanocephalus)
location: Pingree Park Rd (CR63E), Larimer County, Colorado
description: This bird sang in response to recording of Hepatic Tanager. In the field, we heard the bird sing roughly three or four times, but I only recorded a portion. We thought it sounded like Hepatic Tanager, but this is a species not previously observed in our region.  American Robins were present in the vicinity. The mystery bird was never seen and only sang briefly. Habitat was mixed juniper and ponderosa pine hillside near small grove of aspen. After reviewing sonograms of Hepatic Tanager and American Robin and Black-headed Grosbeak, I believe that our instincts in the field were incorrect and that  this is a weak song of a Black-headed Grosbeak.

title: XC354556 Black-throated Sparrow (Amphispiza bilineata)
location: Texas (near  Sheffield), Terrell County, Texas
description:
Unmodified recording from Independence Creek Preserve captured with my Samsung phone. My campsite was located in the slot between two rocky sloping cliffs. I'd describe the habitat as arid shrub land populated by mesquite and agave, along with scattered patches of short grass and plenty of bare ground.

I awoke to the predawn chorus and immediately started recording. The mystery bird issued its trilling call repeatedly and stole the show. It sounded quite close but still invisible. I assume it was perched in a nearby mesquite. I'm only a beginner but the call seems rather sparrow-like.

title: XC277557 Black Phoebe (Sayornis nigricans)
location: Arcata, Humboldt County, California
description:
This 40 second recording documents 18 calls of Black Phoebe just before it left its night roost. I missed the first 5-10 calls. You can also hear wingbeats shortly after the last call. 

More details of the context of this recording may be found here: <http://ebird.org/ebird/view/checklist?subID=S24871443>

This recording was made with an iPhone 4s with a Sennheiser mic and Røde Rec application. This is an unedited and unmodified recording of the natural spacing of this bird's utterances.
author: Elias Aristides Elias

title: XC277742 Black Phoebe (Sayornis nigricans)
location: Arcata, Humboldt County, California
description:
This 3 minute and 30 second recording documents numerous vocalizations of a unknown age, unknown sex Black Phoebe just before it left its night roost. At the beginning of this recording one can hear a distant Black Phoebe calling, then about 10 seconds into it a closer roosting phoebe makes its first noises of the day. It begins by making a 20 mournful calls then it transitions into a song. This bird vocalizes for about one and a half minutes. There is then a lull in its activity until 2:49 when this bird makes 13 calls over 40 seconds. After which it presumably silently left the roost.

More details of the context of this recording may be found here: <http://ebird.org/ebird/view/checklist?subID=S24883462>

This recording was made with an iPhone 4s with a Sennheiser mic and Røde Rec application. This is an unedited and unmodified recording of the natural spacing of this bird's utterances.
author: Elias Aristides Elias

title: XC288988 Blue Jay (Cyanocitta cristata)
location: Oxford, Lafayette County, Mississippi
description:
A pair of Blue Jays foraging in isolated woody vegetation along the margins of the dry lake bed. Abnormally warm for this date, 77 F. Breezy 5-10mph SW. Distance from microphone ~30 m. 

# Habitat #
State waterfowl refuge along the margins of USACE flood control reservoir. Strip along the lake margins ~1km wide of moist soil grassland with mix of forbs, native warm season grasses (Andropogon, Schyzachyrium, Eragrostis, Aristida, etc.), and some sparse woody vegetation (Cephalanthus, Quercus saplings, etc.) bounded by oak hickory forest and, in places, pine plantation.  Three or four shallow waterfowl impoundments partially flooded in the winter.

title: XC307817 Blue Jay (Cyanocitta cristata)
secondary_labels: ['Cardinalis cardinalis_Northern Cardinal', 'Baeolophus bicolor_Tufted Titmouse', 'Bombycilla cedrorum_Cedar Waxwing']
location: Oxford, Lafayette County, Mississippi
description:
Natural sounds. Initially perched in privet in forest understory. Seemed to be harassing a Red-headed Woodpecker, following it from tree to tree and watching the woodpecker while calling. Multiple sounds including typical call, rattle/growl, and repeated mimicry of Red-shouldered Hawk. All RSHA calls in this cut are from the Blue Jay.

#Habitat#
State waterfowl refuge along the margins of USACE flood control reservoir. Strip along the lake margins ~1km wide of moist soil grassland with mix of forbs, native warm season grasses (Andropogon, Schyzachyrium, Eragrostis, Aristida, etc.), and some sparse woody vegetation (Cephalanthus, Quercus saplings, etc.) bounded by oak hickory forest and, in places, pine plantation.  Three or four shallow waterfowl impoundments partially flooded in the winter.

No edits.

Fostex FR-2 digital recorder with Sennheiser microphone and Telinga pro 22" parabolic reflector.

title: XC315101 Blue Jay (Cyanocitta cristata)
secondary_labels: ['Buteo platypterus_Broad-winged Hawk', 'Turdus migratorius_American Robin', 'Cardinalis cardinalis_Northern Cardinal']
location: Oxford, Lafayette County, Mississippi
description:
Natural sound. Two Blue Jays and an American Robin mobbing a Broad-winged Hawk. All three birds perched on bare limbs in the crown of a tree ~7m above the ground. Note harsh Blue Jay calls at 1:23 and 1:40 as the Blue Jay charged the hawk. Besides the occasional sallies by the Blue Jays, there was no other action or violence besides the calls. 

#Habitat#
29-acre estate centrally located in Oxford, MS consisting of antebellum home surrounded by lawns and adjacent forest. Privet hedges and small thickets divide the grounds into distinct lawn units. Bordered on all sides by mature oak-hickory forest. Forest edge consists of oak spp, hickory spp, red cedar, mulberry, with understory along the edge dominated by privet (Ligustrum sp.). Grounds around the house include isolated trees and manicured hedges. A path from the end of the parking area leads northward ~1 km through the forest to the northern edge of the property abutting the University of Mississippi campus

#Editing#
Edited in Adobe Audition. Butterworth high-pass filter, order 3, cutoff frequency 800Hz

Fostex FR-2 digital recorder with Sennheiser microphone and Telinga pro 22" parabolic reflector.

title: XC314681 Brown-headed Cowbird (Molothrus ater)
location: Oxford, Lafayette County, Mississippi
description:
Natural sound. Two males engaging in alternate displays toward one another from perches on bare limbs in the crown of a large tree. The birds were approximately 30-50 cm apart on adjacent limbs 5-10m away from me. The two would alternately display by spreading wings and tail and vocalizing while facing the other. This cut captures the full interaction from the arrival of the two in the tree  to the retreat of one at the end of this cut.

#Habitat#
29-acre estate centrally located in Oxford, MS consisting of antebellum home surrounded by lawns and adjacent forest. Privet hedges and small thickets divide the grounds into distinct lawn units. Bordered on all sides by mature oak-hickory forest. Forest edge consists of oak spp, hickory spp, red cedar, mulberry, with understory along the edge dominated by privet (Ligustrum sp.). Grounds around the house include isolated trees and manicured hedges. A path from the end of the parking area leads northward ~1 km through the forest to the northern edge of the property abutting the University of Mississippi campus

#Editing#
Adobe Audition. Butterworth high-pass filter, cutoff 2 khz, order 3. A 2-sec announcement on the recording was also removed. 

#Equipment#
Fostex FR-2 digital recorder with Sennheiser microphone and Telinga pro 22" parabolic reflector.
author: J.R. Rigby

title: XC331395 Brown-headed Cowbird (Molothrus ater)
location: Poway, San Diego County, California
description: When the bird was first seen it was difficult to identify what it was due to the fact that it and its "parent" were roosting in dense foliage behind the oak tree near the wire fencing on the lower trail.  When the parent was first seen I thought it was a flycatcher, but when it approached the juvenile cowbird I determined it was too small- it turned out to be a Hutton's Vireo.  This was the first time I have ever seen a Brown-headed Cowbird at this location, and perhaps only the third location where I have seen juveniles in a stage where they are still being fed by host parents.  I can recount a few times I've seen juveniles being fed by California Gnatcatchers, but this is the first time I've seen a Brown-headed Cowbird with a Hutton's Vireo for a host parent.  Since this encounter was a real first by all accounts, I wanted to get documentation to commemorate this find.
background: Acorn Woodpecker (Melanerpes formicivorus)

title: XC297982 Barred Owl (Strix varia)
location: Blake Road, Sidney, Kennebec County, Maine
description:
Previously entered as "unknown" but now identified as a barred owl.  I am leaving the orginal comments below for the sake of completeness. Thank you to everyone for your comments!  --Lance



Unknown sound.  Heard after playing a great horned owl recording.   The sounds continued after I played barred owl, northern saw-whet owl, and long-eared owl recordings.  The source of the sounds moved at least twice during the ~25 minutes that I heard it.

I have heard barred and northern saw-whet owl at this location previously (most recently only about six weeks earlier) but this sound doesn't match any by those species that I've ever heard.  I checked every barred owl recording on Xeno-Canto and in the Cornell Master Set but these vocalizations don't match any of them.  I also checked all the Great Horned Owl and Northern Saw-whet Owl vocalizations in the Cornell Master Set and found nothing that matched.

It's possible that this is not a bird and perhaps a mammal.

Recorded in a wet forest adjacent to agricultural fields.  Sounds of traffic from nearby  interstate 95 are also audible.

Equipment: Sony PCM-M10 recorder and a Sennheiser ME67 microphone.
Modifications to the file: amplified by 10 dB.

**Original post follows**
This owl woke me from sleep in my car when I heard it in my headphones. There was a Great Horned Owl flying around, hootin' it up earlier in the day (around 15:30!), so I know there was one in the area. I'm not familiar enough with owl calls to know that this was a GHO, though, so I thought I'd ask.

I'd upload a longer recording, but really, it was this lone, isolated call, with an hour of silence on either side before the next sound (some leaves falling)

Enjoy the reverb! There are some nice, tall conifers there.

Anyone know?

description: We were on our honeymoon in north Georgia.  We sat on the back porch of our cabin, overlooking the Blue Ridge Mountains and began calling into the woods just after sunset. We were thrilled and carried on a back-and-forth conversation with these noisy nocturnal predators for nearly an hour, full of hoots, wails and caterwauls.  We took a one minute trim of the recording for submission here; it is completely unedited.

description:
This audio was extracted from a video taken with a Canon 7D Mk II camera using the built-in microphone.  I was about 30' away from the bird.  The audio was processed using Adobe Audition CC's "Adaptive Noise Reduction" filter to remove wind noise and mechanical noise below 1kHz.  

Bird was an adult female sitting at the top of a large juniper next to a water treatment pond just before sunrise.  A male was nearby calling back with a similar-sounding call but not during the time of this recording.  A Say's Phoebe in the same juniper is heard calling consistently throughout this recording along with a House Finch and a Bewick's Wren that were somewhere nearby.

location: Portland, Cumberland County, Maine
description:
Recorded on iPhone 5 using EIM-001 microphone and RODE Rec app. Imported to Audacity with minor trim to overall time and High Pass Filter to 2200Hz with a rolloff of 24dB. 

Brown Thrasher sitting about 20 feet over my head in an oak tree. Under the budding canopy which seemed to help amplify/direct the sound.  Capisic Pond is a very healthy marsh/forest environment. 

Subject was sitting and singing nothing else. Once it finished, it relocated across the stream/marsh and started singing again. 

Plumage was fairly standard Brown Thrasher leaning more towards the brown than rufous. Best view was from underneath where the streaking was present but rather light in the middle. Most noticiable feature was the tail which consisted of the two outer most retrices with one interior. The rest were about 1/4th of the way in.

title: XC422943 Black-throated Blue Warbler (Setophaga caerulescens)
location: Gorham, Coos County, New Hampshire
description:
A Mt. Washington Park Ranger indicated this location for possible Bicknell's Thrush.

I made several stops along this Dolly Copp/Pinkham Road which is hotspot named : White Mt. National  Forest--Dolly Copp/Pinkham B Road , Coos County, New Hampshire, US.

Area was an older secondary growth with mixture of pine and deciduous trees.

Windy with leaf noise heard throughout.

Playback of Bicknell's Song used and at third stop at which I was moving higher in elevation along road, an unseen bird vocalized, heard and recorded. 

The sound I am trying to ID is heard  is  three /four notes ending in a higher trill and starts just before 5 second mark of recording and heard 5 times in recording.

There is another bird vocalization in recording on the 1st and 3rd time of  focal point bird's vocalization, which I think is a warbler, Am. Redstart.

Audacity was used to edit recording.  Normalized Max. Amplitude at -3dB.

title: XC202027 Black-throated Green Warbler (Setophaga virens)
secondary_labels: ['Vireo olivaceus_Red-eyed Vireo', 'Helmitheros vermivorum_Worm-eating Warbler', 'Setophaga americana_Northern Parula', 'Setophaga citrina_Hooded Warbler', 'Baeolophus bicolor_Tufted Titmouse']
location: William B. Bankhead National Forest (near  Moulton), Sipsey Wilderness Area, FS Rd. 208, Lawrence County, Alabama
description:
Unusual song-type for species (as far as I know), first part is typical BTNW, second part is somewhat reminiscent of a Cerulean Warbler.  In the recording, there are at least three counter-singing individuals, maybe four but did not keep notes at the time.  This is the only location in the Bankhead National Forest Sipsey Wilderness Area I've heard this song type.  First noticed it at this location in May of 2013.  Interestingly a Cerulean Warbler was found singing and photographed at this location 2013-05-09.  However I wonder if subsequent reports to eBird of Cerulean Warbler at this location may have been these atypical BTNWs.  Both times I've visited this site in 2013 and 2014 I've never had CERW  but have had visual of BTNWs singing this song type.

Recorded using iPhone 5s internal microphone and the Rode Rec. app.
background: Red-eyed Vireo (Vireo olivaceus); Worm-eating Warbler (Helmitheros vermivorum); Northern Parula (Setophaga americana); Hooded Warbler (Setophaga citrina); Tufted Titmouse (Baeolophus bicolor)

title: XC133590 Black-throated Grey Warbler (Setophaga nigrescens)
location: Coquitlam, Greater Vancouver, British Columbia
description:
Recorded using an iPhone 4 Voice Memos app (no accessories).  Bird was in the canopy an estimated 10m to 20m away and was not seen initially but was seen clearly while singing the next day.  Some background sounds are from nearby road and school yard.  Singing occurs at 0:04, 0:24, 1:00, 1:43 and 2:14.  The recording was normalized and HP filtered at a frequency of 3000Hz with a roll-off of 24 db/octave using Audacity.

There was some initial confusion with a Magnolia Warbler which would have been rare in the sighting area.  Note the similarity of the song with this Magnolia Warbler recording from Quebec:  XC133254.
author: KevinHHood

title: XC141677 Black-throated Grey Warbler (Setophaga nigrescens)
location: Coquitlam, Greater Vancouver, British Columbia
description:
Fledglings begging to Adult:  A male adult Black-throated Grey Warbler followed by two fledglings were moving around in the low-to-mid canopy of a small group of cottonwoods about 30 to 40 feet in height.  The recording was made from a stationary location about 20 to 30 feet from the birds on average.

A set of 13 photographs with synchronization timing with this recording and showing from 1 to all 3 of the birds can be found at the following URL:  <http://www.flickr.com/photos/94309556@N05/sets/72157634504521314/>.

You can hear the camera shutter in the recording as I was taking the pictures.  The camera shutter signature on the sonograms was how I eventually synchronized the pictures to the recording.

One of the more interesting parts of the recording starts around 0:48 and continues for about 25 seconds.  At around 1:02 there is a short 2 to 3 second burst of juvenile calling followed, starting just after 1:05, by a quite period of almost 4 seconds.  During this noisy-then-quiet period the fledglings appear to be actually getting some food from the adult - see [Image 540](http://flickr.com/gp/94309556@N05/k54yxo) which was taken at the beginning of this quiet period.

The weather was sunny and warm with little wind.  Recording was high-pass filtered with a cutoff at 3Kh to remove street sounds.  The original recording is just over 8 minutes in length.
background: Black-capped Chickadee (Poecile atricapillus)
author: Kevin Hood

title: XC144071 Black-throated Grey Warbler (Setophaga nigrescens)
secondary_labels: ['Spinus psaltria_Lesser Goldfinch', 'Polioptila caerulea_Blue-gray Gnatcatcher', 'Poecile gambeli_Mountain Chickadee', 'Contopus sordidulus_Western Wood-Pewee', 'Phainopepla nitens_Phainopepla']
location: Icehouse Canyon Trailhead, San Gabriel Mountains, San Bernardino County, California
description:
Fledgling black-throated gray warbler begging.  The young bird is fed by one of its parents 35 seconds into the recording.  The birds were in canyon live oaks near a creek.  Photographed.  We watched them at a range of as little as 3 meters.  They were moving around a lot between about 1/2 meter to 2 meters above the ground.  The parent did not vocalize.

Other trees in the area: incense cedar, white alder, bigcone Douglas fir, California bigleaf maple, chaparral species such as yucca, manzanita, and scrub oak.

Modifications to the recording: I cropped off a few seconds at the end and amplified it by a factor of two.

Equipment: Olympus LS-10 equipped with a Sennheiser MKE-400 short shotgun microphone.
background: Lesser Goldfinch (Spinus psaltria); Blue-grey Gnatcatcher (Polioptila caerulea); Mountain Chickadee (Poecile gambeli); Western Wood Pewee (Contopus sordidulus); Phainopepla (Phainopepla nitens)

title: XC377144 Black-throated Grey Warbler (Setophaga nigrescens)
location: Washington, Skamania County, Washington
description:
Originally uploaded as a mystery, this is an example of the typical song of a Black-Throated Grey Warbler in the Mt Adams area of Washington state, USA.

Original post:
This bird was recorded just after dawn in the Gifford-Pinchot National Forest/ Mt Adams Recreational Area as part of a soundscape. I've been able to identify other species in the recording, but am having a bit of difficulty with this one. The  birds it mostly closely resembles in song to aren't the area. The locally-known breeding birds it is similar to (i.e. Yellow Warbler) have enough differences in vocalizations that I'm doubting my ID. It's an extremely common bird in this area, but  one I don't yet know personally.

Recording characteristics: amplified, some filtering out of the low-end to focus on the bird itself. No edits. First vocalization is within one second, followed by five more at 10-15 second intervals.

Vegetation: coniferous forest, mostly douglas fir

Bird unseen

Thanks for your help!
author: Andy Martin

#Habitat#
29-acre estate centrally located in Oxford, MS consisting of antebellum home surrounded by lawns and adjacent forest. Privet hedges and small thickets divide the grounds into distinct lawn units. A path from the end of the parking area leads northward ~1 km through the forest to the northern edge of the property abutting the University of Mississippi campus

Edited in Adobe Audition. Butterworth high-pass filter, order 3, cutoff frequency 1kHz

#Equipment#
Fostex FR-2 digital recorder with Sennheiser microphone and Telinga pro 22" parabolic reflector.

Lakeshore park with open lawns and some large trees, mostly water oak (*Quercus nigra*) and loblolly pine (*Pinus taeda*).

title: XC205952 Blue-winged Warbler (Vermivora cyanoptera)
location: Welchester Tree Grant Park, Golden, Jefferson County, Colorado
description:
Somewhat unusual, buzzy three-note form (Golden-wing type) of natural song, given by bird foraging in moderately dense foliage near creek. Noise below 100Hz filtered.

I spoke with (over email) Rachel Vallender who studies BWWA/GWWA complexes. She listened to my recording and wrote this in reply: "This bird is singing a slightly odd GWWA song. I agree that it's not the typical (type I) beee-BUZZZZ of the BWWA, or the bee-buzz-buzz-buzz of a GWWA, but I've certainly had lots of GWWA that sound like this. And I've definitely come across BWWA that sing GWWA songs, and vice versa. So this bird was a phenotypic BWWA?"(The answer is yes, as best as I could tell visually and from photos other birders shared.)
background: Black-billed Magpie (Pica hudsonia)
author: Eric DeFonso

title: XC127624 Canada Goose (Branta canadensis)
location: Powderhorn Park, Minneapolis, Hennepin, Minnesota
description:
Two pairs of early-returning geese on the ice of a still-frozen lake in an urban park.  The closest pair was approximately 10m away, the other pair about 30m.  One member of the nearby pair (presumably the female) was mostly silent and was sitting down on the ice for most of the recording.  The other goose (presumably the male) was doing most of the vocalizing.  Periodically he would give a grating crescendo call with a loud finish (e.g. heard clearly at 3:04.5, but present throughout the recording).  While doing this call, he would throw his head back, pointed up to the sky.  Immediately after these calls, he generally would nip at the back or neck of the other member of the pair.

Calls from a member of the other pair (presumably the male) in the background, slowly getting closer. One member of each pair had been observed fighting eachother several minutes before.

Airplane interlude about halfway through the recording. Light filtering below 400Hz.
author: Jonathon Jongsma

description:
A large flock of Canada Geese taking off. I believe most of the birds in this flock were parvipes ("Lesser") Canada Geese, but there were also larger (subspecies moffitti?) In the old days this would have been an "obvious" or "easy" flock of "Canada Geese." Now we're dealing with perhaps two species and probably two or three subspecies in the recording. Again, I believe most of the birds audible here are parvipes ("Lesser") Canada Geese.

No edits.

location: OSU's Waterman Farm wood lot, Columbus, Franklin County, Ohio
description:
Recorded along the southeast margin of the wood lot on the Ohio State University experimental farm (Waterman Farm; limited access) located in urban Columbus, OH adjacent to the OSU campus (see map). The Canada Warbler was first seen and heard along a stream inside the wood lot, then moved to the edge of the wood lot while I ran back to my car to get recording equipment. There, it was mostly in honey suckle bushes or adjacent lower branches of trees along the edge of the wood lot.  I was pleasantly surprised to have a Mourning Warbler do the audio-equivalent of "photo bombing" my Canada Warbler recording!  All of this session's Mourning Warbler recordings: at the end of XC179676 and throughout XC179679 (XC179681 cropped from XC179679). All of this session's Canada Warbler recordings: XC179676, XC179679 (XC179681 cropped from XC179679), and XC179691. Audacity software was used for post-processing of recordings (signal:noise reduction via high pass filter, then amplification).  Eastern Chipmunk also audible in the background.

title: XC330125 Canyon Wren (Catherpes mexicanus)
location: Poway, San Diego County, California
description: Ever since I first identified that there were resident Canyon Wrens both at Lake Poway and Blue Sky Ecological Reserve, I have been attempting to obtain visual and auditory proof of their presence, but they sing and call fairly infrequently, and are more cryptic than the other wrens seen in the surrounding areas.  However, on this day I heard and saw one bird on the rock pile near the trail junction merging with Blue Sky Ecological Reserve.  Fortunately, the bird continued to call and sing for several minutes and even made appearances on the rocks.  Although I was finally able to get a recording, I was unable to get a photograph due to its swiftness.  I made a few whistles and hisses to try and keep it out of its den, and although it kept it around longer, this was still not enough to snap a picture.  The most audible calls and singing occur from 0:43 onward.

A path from the end of the parking area leads northward ~1 km through the forest to the northern edge of the property abutting the University of Mississippi campus

secondary_labels: ['Poecile atricapillus_Black-capped Chickadee', 'Sayornis nigricans_Black Phoebe', 'Spinus psaltria_Lesser Goldfinch']
location: Arcata, Humboldt County, California
description:
This 1 minutes and 36 second recording documents approximately 45 alarm calls from a single adult unsexed Cedar Waxwing. This waxwing had just flown in and saw me and looped around to land at the top of a Red Alder. I suspect that there is a nest site nearby as I have heard a distressed waxwing nearby recently. There is one call type exhibited from the focal individual: a whistled falling ‘see’ similar to several species of thrush alarm notes. However there is a point in this recording when a unassociated flock of three Cedar Waxwings flew over the very tree that the focal waxwing is perched in.

More details of the context of this recording may be found here: <http://ebird.org/ebird/view/checklist?subID=S24796624>

This recording was made with an iPhone 5s with the built-in mic and Røde Rec application. This is an unedited and unmodified recording of the natural spacing of this bird's utterances.
background: Black-capped Chickadee (Poecile atricapillus); Black Phoebe (Sayornis nigricans); Lesser Goldfinch (Spinus psaltria)

description:
Perched in the bare limbs in the crown of  a deciduous tree. FOS this fall.

State waterfowl refuge along the margins of USACE flood control reservoir. Strip along the lake margins ~1km wide of moist soil grassland with mix of forbs, native warm season grasses (Andropogon, Schyzachyrium, Eragrostis, Aristida, etc.), and some sparse woody vegetation (Cephalanthus, Quercus saplings, etc.) bounded by oak hickory forest and, in places, pine plantation.  Three or four shallow waterfowl impoundments partially flooded in the winter.

#Editing#
Edited in Adobe Audition. Butterworth high-pass filter, order 3, cutoff frequency **6 kHz**. 

#Equipment#
Fostex FR-2 digital recorder with Sennheiser microphone and Telinga pro 22" parabolic reflector.

title: XC288985 Chipping Sparrow (Spizella passerina)
location: Oxford, Lafayette County, Mississippi
description:
Perched on chain link fence. 

# Habitat #
State waterfowl refuge along the margins of USACE flood control reservoir. Strip along the lake margins ~1km wide of moist soil grassland with mix of forbs, native warm season grasses (Andropogon, Schyzachyrium, Eragrostis, Aristida, etc.), and some sparse woody vegetation (Cephalanthus, Quercus saplings, etc.) bounded by oak hickory forest and, in places, pine plantation.  Three or four shallow waterfowl impoundments partially flooded in the winter.

# Editing #
Adobe Audition. Butterworth high-pass filter, cutoff 2 khz, order 3

# Equipment #
Fostex FR-2 digital field recorder with Telinga Pro 22" parabolic reflector

description: No modification of the recording.  The vocalizations in this recording are of 3 Chimney Swifts being hand raised.  The first part is the begging call which I believe it would be safe to characterize as normal.  The last part of the recording features a different vocalization, more like growling as the birds feel threatened.  That sound was induced by gently shaking the box in which they are being raised.  The young cling vertically to a towel or blanket placed in the box.  The birds were all collected from homeowners who found them having slipped from a perch in their chimneys.  My thanks to Nicole Janke for assisting in this effort.

title: XC307685 Common Grackle (Quiscalus quiscula)
location: Oxford, Lafayette County, Mississippi
description:
Natural sound. Audio from one individual perched in 15-20m tree and joined by two other individuals.

#Habitat#
State waterfowl refuge along the margins of USACE flood control reservoir. Strip along the lake margins ~1km wide of moist soil grassland with mix of forbs, native warm season grasses (Andropogon, Schyzachyrium, Eragrostis, Aristida, etc.), and some sparse woody vegetation (Cephalanthus, Quercus saplings, etc.) bounded by oak hickory forest and, in places, pine plantation.  Three or four shallow waterfowl impoundments partially flooded in the winter.

#Editing#
No edits.

#Equipment#
Fostex FR-2 digital recorder with Sennheiser microphone and Telinga pro 22" parabolic reflector.

The bird was giving 'boom' dives and higher, shallower dives (with an abbreviated vocalization at the bottom instead of a boom), but the boom dives typically were performed below the edge of the library building, where I couldn't get the boom on-mic. Most of the vocalizations are given with a quick flutter of wingbeats, lifting the bird a bit from its line of flight. title: XC253133 Northern Raven (Corvus corax)
location: Inishbofin, Co. Galway
description: These raucous squawks were produced by members of a nine-strong troupe (I believe two family parties were involved) that settled on the roof of a farmer's home on a Sunday morning at 0640hrs. The racket was deafening and the clip was recorded roughly ten minutes after the birds arrived. I made the recording from an adjoining cottage: so you can imagine the volume for the people in the house upon whose roof the birds were sitting. The farmer had buried a dead sheep nearby the day before and the Ravens had smelled the rotten corpse. However, it was too deep for them to disinter. The noise made by the horde caused some calling among other birds in the farmer's garden: such as juvenile Blackbirds [examples at 0:03 and 0:04], Goldfinches [examples at 0:27, 0:44 and 1:06] and a Wren [example at 0:18]. Skylark song can be heard as a backdrop from 0:06 onwards and is best from 1:15 to the end. A Corncrake calls from time to time. Although faint, the Corncrake can be detected after 0:59 for about five seconds. The gull cry at 0:52 (for the next three seconds) are from a Herring Gull.
author: Anthony McGeehan

title: XC478625 Cooper's Hawk (Accipiter cooperii)
location: Cerro La Bufa, San Sebastián del Oeste, Jalisco
description:
When I heard this bird in the field, I reacted to it spontaneously by saying: Eared Quetzal! Unfortunately the origin of the sound never showed itself, why I never got a confirmation, and have after that not been able to find any similar recordings. There certainly aren't any recordings here on xeno-canto of Eared Quetzal that sounds like this, why I now have to think that it is not such a bird.

However, the strange thing is, that before having this experience I had been studying up on that exact species, and went exactly there in hope of finding it. This was based on information from an American guide who has seen it at La Bufa on several occasions. I remember that I studied sounds and behavior of the species, and based on that I got to the spontaneous conclusion when I heard this sound, that it was an Eared Quetzal. Today I have no idea where I learned this call from. But I must have heard it before, otherwise I don't think my reaction would have been so swift and doubtless.
Later I've heard it again once on the volcano Nevado de Colima in southern Jalisco, but again didn't see the creature that made the sound.

I started to think that it was an Mountain Trogon, but there seems to be no similar recording under that species either here on xeno-canto, and the same goes for the woodpeckers of the region.

Is it not a bird, or which species have I overlooked?
It's the two-part call you hear at sec 13 and 39. Ek  eheheheheh
The time of day is estimated.

Thanks for your help.
author: Jesper Bay Jacobsen

title: XC195844 Dark-eyed Junco (Junco hyemalis)
secondary_labels: ['Melospiza melodia_Song Sparrow', "Selasphorus sasin_Allen's Hummingbird", 'Sturnus vulgaris_European Starling', 'Zonotrichia leucophrys_White-crowned Sparrow', 'Anas platyrhynchos_Mallard']
location: Palace of Fine Arts (near  San Francisco), San Francisco County, California
description:
Three dependent juvenile plumaged Dark-eyed Junco (Oregon) were in area and were being fed by an adult Dark-eyed Junco (Oregon). If I recall they had nearly full-grown tails and were perhaps a week out of the nest. This recording was made at the Palace of Fine Arts, San Francisco, California (WGS84 37.802340, -122.448028). These birds were flitting around on the ground at my feet and were being fed by an adult. Two juvenile call types were recorded in this 134 second long recording: first was a buzzy begging note (quite variable) sometime given singly, other times repeated and when very excited (such as when adult approached with food) it was given rapidly. More rarely a second call was given—a brief chip—likely an analogue to the adult Chack note.  The adult Chack call was described in the BNA account as: Chack, also interpretable as tik, stip (Fig. 2F): wide-frequency, short-duration single syllable, often uttered near ground predator (Hostetter 1961); general alarm call during winter (Whitney 1968).

This recording was made with an iPhone 5s with the built-in microphone and the Røde Rec application. This recording has not been modified in any manner. This recording has some city type noises in the background.

Dark-eyed Junco (Oregon): 

begging: begins at 0:00  with an intense volley of begging is at 1:29
chipping: begins at 1:10 and at times blends into a begging note.

Song Sparrow (song): 0:00, 0:15, 0:31, 0:39

Allen’s Hummingbird: 0:15

European Starling: 0:53, 0:58, 0:59

White-crowned Sparrow (song): 1:04, 1:17

Mallard 1:36
background: Song Sparrow (Melospiza melodia); Allen's Hummingbird (Selasphorus sasin); Common Starling (Sturnus vulgaris); White-crowned Sparrow (Zonotrichia leucophrys); Mallard (Anas platyrhynchos)

Strip along the lake margins ~1km wide of moist soil grassland with mix of forbs, native warm season grasses (Andropogon, Schyzachyrium, Eragrostis, Aristida, etc.), and some sparse woody vegetation (Cephalanthus, Quercus saplings, etc.) bounded by oak hickory forest and, in places, pine plantation.  Three or four shallow waterfowl impoundments partially flooded in the winter.

#Editing#
Edited in Adobe Audition. Butterworth high-pass filter, order 3, cutoff frequency 700 Hz. 

#Equipment#
Fostex FR-2 digital recorder with Sennheiser microphone and Telinga pro 22" parabolic reflector.

title: XC324884 Downy Woodpecker (Dryobates pubescens)
location: Bloomingdale, Chatham County, Georgia
description:
I originally posted this file as Hairy Woodpecker, a species not yet verifiably identified in this coastal county.  After creating a spectrogram of my recording and comparing it to those of Hairy and Downy I created from Cornell I concluded Downy.
 
I heard two birds calling and saw them land in clear woodpecker fashion on the limbs of a dead snag, in a pine tree, vocalizing all the while. Although my original intent in exploring this new area was to find Hairy Woodpecker, I was there recording frogs this morning. As a result I was able to turn the microphone on the pair and get about one minute of vocalization. Photography was not possible with poor lighting and distance.

I used a Sound Devices 722 with a Sennheiser ME67 long shotgun microphone. The file as been altered for clarity, including increasing gain to -06 from the original -16, deleting human artifacts, and employing a conservative high pass filter, and equally conservative noise reduction in Audacity to diminish ambient distractions. The cadence of vocalizations is largely untouched. The original WAV file is available.
background: Northern Parula (Setophaga americana); Carolina Wren (Thryothorus ludovicianus)
author: Russ Wigh

title: XC190996 American Dusky Flycatcher (Empidonax oberholseri)
location: Lakeshore, Fresno County, California
description:
This is a recording of 3 juvenile Dusky Flycatchers foraging close to the ground in a conifer woodland. These birds appeared to be independent as no parental types were visiting but recordist did not spend a long time with these birds. Initially these birds are about 10 meters from the microphone, they then flew to about 25 meters away. Two call types are exhibited: one is a repeated House Sparrow like “cheep" and the other is a flight note of a couple of different types. 

This recording was made with an iPhone 5s with the built-in microphone and the Røde Rec application. This recording has not been modified in any manner. There is some talking by the recordist.

Dusky Flycatcher: cheeps 0:01, 0:03, 0:04.5, 0:06, 0:07, 0:09, 0:11, 0:12 (a more distant individual), 0:13.5, 0:14, 0:15.6, 0:17.5 (17.9), 0:22.5 (23.129), 0:23 (several cheeps at 23.1, 24.1, 24.6 (distant), 25.2, 26.3, 27.8

Dusky Flycatcher: flight notes 0:18 a rapid series of doubled chips at 18.3, 18.7, 19.4, followed by a different single chip note at 19.9 and then a doubled chip at 20.85, again followed by single chips at 21.15, and 21.47

Mountain Chickadee: 0:10, 0:15.33
background: Mountain Chickadee (Poecile gambeli)

description: Heard the bird calling outside my office window at the visitor center and got 20-second recording. By the time I ran outside with the camera it was gone. Recorded with iPhone SE, amplification, high pass filter, and noise reduction used in Audacity. Casual in Maricopa County (this would be only 3rd or 4th record). Presumably of the nominate S.s. sialis population, which is migratory (the 'Azure' bluebird of southeastern AZ and the Sierra Madre Occidental is believed to be sedentary). title: XC158055 Eastern Phoebe (Sayornis phoebe)
location: Malibu Legacy Park, Los Angeles County, California
description:
Natural vocalizations by an eastern phoebe.  Malibu legacy park is an open area with scattered bushes and native grasses that surround a small wetland.  The bird was about 10 meters from me when it was vocalizing.

Eastern phoebe is a rare bird at this location.  Entered into Xeno-Canto primarily for documentation.

Photographed extensively.

The eastern phoebe often chased a black phoebe while we watched.  Both species are audible on the recording. 

Abundant noise from vehicles on Pacific Coast Highway is also audible.

Equipment: Olympus LS-10S equipped with a Sennheiser MKE-400.
File modifications: cropped at both ends.
background: Black Phoebe (Sayornis nigricans)

title: XC316544 Eastern Phoebe (Sayornis phoebe)
location: Montréal, Communauté-Urbaine-de-Montréal, Québec
description:
The record was filtered to reduce noise at low frequency (water stream from big hose) and noise reduction was  applied lightly from an audio program (Audacity).This is a unique recording of this bird.
This bird is adult and  probably she is nesting. In this park with  many big trees and bush close to a pond, she was seen and heard on a branch, 15 meters above microphone when she reacted of Cooper Hawk fly by her nest in an old house roof. So her typical song was repeated at intervals of 1.5 s. and the second song was a high tonality chip at 1 s. A photograph is taken to confirm identity. This was recorded half an hour before sunset, may 12th 2016.   Daylight was good and no wind and no rain or humidity.

title: XC307795 Eastern Towhee (Pipilo erythrophthalmus)
location: Oxford, Lafayette County, Mississippi
description:
Natural sound. Perched in the top of an isolated 4m locust tree approximately 40m away singing over an open grassland.

#Habitat#
State waterfowl refuge along the margins of USACE flood control reservoir. Strip along the lake margins ~1km wide of moist soil grassland with mix of forbs, native warm season grasses (Andropogon, Schyzachyrium, Eragrostis, Aristida, etc.), and some sparse woody vegetation (Cephalanthus, Quercus saplings, etc.) bounded by oak hickory forest and, in places, pine plantation.  Three or four shallow waterfowl impoundments partially flooded in the winter.

#Editing#
No edits.

#Equipment#
Fostex FR-2 digital recorder with Sennheiser microphone and Telinga pro 22" parabolic reflector.
background: Field Sparrow (Spizella pusilla)

secondary_labels: ['Vireo olivaceus_Red-eyed Vireo', 'Cardinalis cardinalis_Northern Cardinal', 'Hylocichla mustelina_Wood Thrush', 'Piranga rubra_Summer Tanager', 'Vireo griseus_White-eyed Vireo']
location: Oxford, Lafayette County, Mississippi
description:
Natural sound. Call at e.g., 0:01, 0:10, and 0:24. Bird foraging in a tulip poplar and surrounding trees ~5-7m above the ground. Sallying from a branch to capture insects in the air, sometimes returning to the same perch, sometimes perching on a new branch. 

#Habitat#
29-acre estate centrally located in Oxford, MS consisting of antebellum home surrounded by lawns and adjacent forest. Privet hedges and small thickets divide the grounds into distinct lawn units. Bordered on all sides by mature oak-hickory forest. Forest edge consists of oak spp, hickory spp, red cedar, mulberry, with understory along the edge dominated by privet (Ligustrum sp.). Grounds around the house include isolated trees and manicured hedges. A path from the end of the parking area leads northward ~1 km through the forest to the northern edge of the property abutting the University of Mississippi campus

#Editing#
Edited in Adobe Audition. Butterworth high-pass filter, order 3, cutoff frequency 800 Hz

#Equipment#
Fostex FR-2 digital recorder with Sennheiser microphone and Telinga pro 22" parabolic reflector.

location: Oxford, Lafayette County, Mississippi
description:
Natural vocalization. High flight call at 0:00, 0:10, and 0:28. This bird flushed from the tall grass on my approach and perched in a 1.5m tall locust sapling where it called several times before flying away. Distance from microphone ~5m.

#Habitat#
State waterfowl refuge along the margins of USACE flood control reservoir. Strip along the lake margins ~1km wide of moist soil grassland with mix of forbs, native warm season grasses (Andropogon, Schyzachyrium, Eragrostis, Aristida, etc.), and some sparse woody vegetation (Cephalanthus, Quercus saplings, etc.) bounded by oak hickory forest and, in places, pine plantation.  Three or four shallow waterfowl impoundments partially flooded in the winter.

#Editing#
Adobe Audition. Butterworth high-pass filter, cutoff *4 kHz*, order 3

#Equipment#
Fostex FR-2 digital recorder with Sennheiser microphone and Telinga pro 22" parabolic reflector.

title: XC393547 Grey-crowned Rosy Finch (Leucosticte tephrocotis)
location: Ellensburg, Kittitas County, Washington
description: Flight calls from a flock of approximately 150 Grey-crowned Rosy Finches near the summit of Baldy in the Yakima River Canyon. This recording was taken with and iPhone 6  and only a few seconds contained flight calls uncontaminated by wind noise. This recording was high passed at 1000 Hz with a 6 dB roll-off and a Hamming window to reduce wind noise and the resulting recording was normalized.
author: Walter Szeliga

title: XC395826 Grey-crowned Rosy Finch (Leucosticte tephrocotis)
location: Ellensburg, Kittitas County, Washington
description: Solitary Gray-crowned Rosy Finch perched on a fence post at the top of the Umtanum Ridge Trail. There was a strong, multi-day inversion and the bird was a few hundred vertical feet into the freezing fog cloud-bank. The effect of being above such a strong inversion layer and in the cloud-bank resulted in an eerie, absolute silence. This was manifest on the recording as extreme "tape hiss" which was the result of the iPhone microphone attempting to gain correct for the conditions. To reduce this "tape hiss", the recording was low-pass filtered at 5000 Hz with a 6 dB roll-off and then high-pass filtered at 1000 Hz with a 6 dB roll-off and then amplified. The recording was obtained with an iPhone 6 using the Voice Memos app.
author: Walter Szeliga

Grounds around the house include isolated trees and manicured hedges. A path from the end of the parking area leads northward ~1 km through the forest to the northern edge of the property abutting the University of Mississippi campus.

Audacity high-pass filter with a fairly drastic 24 dB rolloff 2 kHz as highway noise swamped the high frequency chatter.

location: Mt. Ibuki, Shiga Prefecture
description:
Possible voice of this species.  I am familiar with the voice of this
species through various videos and this sounded very similar
to them.  The resultant recording was not so clear as I expected,
possibly due to the great distance from the observing location
and background cicada sounds.  The voice has a descending tone
from 3 to 2 kKz (at 0.5s), but the duration seems to be a bit short.
A young bird was witnessed to fly over this location
15 min before and I pointed the microphone to the direction
where the bird was observed.  This place is over the cliff and
other birds were only rarely heard.  I provide this recording
for consideration.  Band-pass filtering has been applied.

location: Mt. Ibuki, Shiga Prefecture
description:
Suspected ID.  The voice was heard when we were in the fog.
We couldn't recognize the bird after the clearance of the fog.
The voice was heard from the direction where there is
a frequently used perching site (it is not directly seen from
the place of observation) according to a local observer.
The voice is different from typical adult calls, and it may
have been from a juvenile bird.  The voice is less structured,
but has some (preceding before the main note) structure
characteristic to this species at least in two notes at 8.0s and 8.9s.
A mimic by an Eurasian jay cannot be completely excluded
but I could not hear jay calls in the corresponding distance.

title: XC385227 Golden Eagle (Aquila chrysaetos)
location: Ishikawa Zoo, Nomi-shi, Ishikawa Prefecture
description:
Although this is a voice from an individual in the zoo, I provide this recording
for the reference and research in the absence of a freely available
secure recording of Aquila chrysaetos japonica (there are several
videos in YouTube).  The number of this subspecies is estimated
to be 500 (according to the page of Society for Research of Golden Eagle Japan)
and there are only 150-200 pairs.  The successful breeding rate is
very low (10-20% for well-studied pairs) and we probably have little
chance to hear the voice in the wild (considering that the birds are
most vocal in the presence of begging juveniles).
Although I have uploaded some suspected vocalizations of this
species, I provide this since I consider this recording represents the most typical voice
of this (sub)species.
The recording was made when the zoo was closed and I noticed
the voice at the entrance.  It took some time to prepare the recorder
and I only managed to take two phrases.  Although the bird was
not directly seen, the ID is secure.  It was likely that the bird begged.
(It is said that recording of this species is difficult even in zoos).

(Later comment):
I found that recently recorded calls are available on the
website:
http://www.bird-research.jp/1_shiryo/nakigoe.html
See at イヌワシ

title: XC135970 Great Egret (Ardea alba)
location: Savannah, Chatham, Georgia
description:
gaggle of begging calls at a rookery of 100-plus nests on and island in the middle of a suburban lagoon.  Interspersed are the calls of squabbling adults.  The rookery is host to Double-crested Cormorant, Anhinga, Snowy Egret and Common Gallinule as breeders.  Others regularly on the island in surrounding trees are Black-crowned Night-Heron, Wood Stork and both Black and Turkey Vulture.

The habitat on the rookery consists of scrubby trees on which nests of sticks are constructed, and higher grasses.  Most of the behavior centered around the nestlings begging for food.  Most of the nestlings are still in the down stage, although feathers are appearing.

title: XC234534 Greater Yellowlegs (Tringa melanoleuca)
location: Sugar Land, Fort Bend County, Texas
description:
This guy is was in the shores of the lake alone and flight away when I got to close to it. I could record part of the singing while it was flying away. At first I was thinking this might be a Lesser Yellowlegs (*Tringa flaviceps*)or a Solitaire Sanpiper (*Tringa solitaria*); But the pitch of the singing is way more similar to a the Lesser Yellowlegs. Now, the thing is that I find that the pitch is really similar to the Greater Yellowlegs (*Tringa melanoleuca*) too. So now I'm not really sure to which bird this corresponds, I'm given to think that it is a Lesser Yellowlegs but I'm not sure so it would be good to confirm.

Another thing: should be this classified as a alarm call or flight call?

title: XC195626 Great Horned Owl (Bubo virginianus)
location: Three Points, Angeles National Forest, Los Angeles County, California
description:
"Wac wac" call in response to playing a northern saw-whet owl recording.  A short time after this recording ended, I started hearing female squawk and male territorial calls from the same direction.  I didn't play any great horned owl vocalizations.  This is an uncommon GHOW vocalization, and to identify it, I compared this recording with one on the "Voices of North American Owls" CD.  I also compared the recording with spotted owl, long-eared owl, and even mule deer (which I saw nearby) recordings and was able to exclude those species.  A faint western screech owl is audible in the background and earlier I had also heard some whines from a northern saw-whet owl.

Habitat: Edge of an open forest with Coulter pine, canyon live oak, bigcone Douglas Fir, incense cedar, and chaparral  species.

Equipment: Olympus LS-10 with a Telinga 22 inch dish and a Sennheiser ME62 microphone.

Modifications to the file: cropped and amplified by 10 dB.

title: XC253709 Green Heron (Butorides virescens)
location: Arcata, Humboldt County, California
description:
This 1+ minute long recording documents 7 vocalizations of a Green Heron. The vocalist was not seen uttering these noises. However, there were Green Herons in the area and even in the tree that this vocalist was in. The sound source was within 15 meters of the microphone. This file begins with all 7 vocs back to back for comparative purposes and to display well on the spectrogram. This prelude is followed by a second of silence. What follows that is the unedited and unmodified recording of the natural spacing of this bird’s utterances.

The first 4 and then 7th calls have a introductory element which is reminiscent of the typical “skow” vocalization but softer and not as loud. That introductory element grades into a low-pitched growl. The 5th and 6th calls begin at 0:05.3 lack the introductory element and seem to be solely the growl. Could be the male song as described in the account "During breeding season, advertising calls or song by male are show-ch or ow-ch (Townsend 1928). Low-pitched skow call given from top of tree or other perch with bill up at 45° angle."

Additional details regarding context may be found at: <http://ebird.org/ebird/view/checklist?subID=S23971407>

This recording was made with an iPhone 5s with the on-board microphone and Røde Rec application.
background: Warbling Vireo (Vireo gilvus)
author: Elias Aristides Elias

title: XC253773 Green Heron (Butorides virescens)
secondary_labels: ["Catharus ustulatus_Swainson's Thrush", 'Icteria virens_Yellow-breasted Chat', 'Poecile atricapillus_Black-capped Chickadee']
location: Arcata, Humboldt County, California
description:
This 20-second long recording documents 2 flight displays of an adult Green Heron. This heron did an aerial display within the canopy of an Red Alder. It only made a mechanical noise with its wings. This heron had just flown into the tree from the river bed. It landed and perched for a few seconds. It then flew with the body held at a 45˚ angle and a hunched back. The wings were not lifted much above horizontal but were deeply flapped under the body. The wings were quite flared. This noise was created in the downflap. This bird flapped 10 times. This bird landed perhaps 5 meters above where it took off and disappeared from view and was not seen again. At 0:19 it made a second display also with 10 flaps. The sound source was within 15 meters of the microphone. This cut is an unedited and unmodified recording of the natural spacing of this bird’s display.

This is what the Birds of North America account has to say: "Flap Flight Display is highest intensity of flight displays, where male lurches through air with exaggerated flapping producing whom-whoom-whoom sound, neck crooked, legs dangling, skow ing, crest, neck, and scapular feathers erect, sometimes giving roo-roo calls before landing."

Davis, Jr., W. E. and J. A. Kushlan. 1994. Green Heron (Butorides virescens), The Birds of North America Online (A. Poole, Ed.). Ithaca: Cornell Lab of Ornithology; Retrieved from the Birds of North America Online: http://bna.birds.cornell.edu/bna/species/129

Additional details regarding context may be found at: <http://ebird.org/ebird/view/checklist?subID=S23971407>

This recording was made with an iPhone 5s with on-board microphone and Røde Rec application.
background: Swainson's Thrush (Catharus ustulatus); Yellow-breasted Chat (Icteria virens); Black-capped Chickadee (Poecile atricapillus)
author: Elias Aristides Elias

title: XC315103 Grey Catbird (Dumetella carolinensis)
location: Oxford, Lafayette County, Mississippi
description:
Natural sound. Bird not visible. Calls coming from within dense privet along an ephemeral stream bed in the forest understory.

#Habitat#
29-acre estate centrally located in Oxford, MS consisting of antebellum home surrounded by lawns and adjacent forest. Privet hedges and small thickets divide the grounds into distinct lawn units. Bordered on all sides by mature oak-hickory forest. Forest edge consists of oak spp, hickory spp, red cedar, mulberry, with understory along the edge dominated by privet (Ligustrum sp.). Grounds around the house include isolated trees and manicured hedges. A path from the end of the parking area leads northward ~1 km through the forest to the northern edge of the property abutting the University of Mississippi campus

#Editing#
Edited in Adobe Audition. Butterworth high-pass filter, order 3, cutoff frequency 800Hz

#Equipment#
Fostex FR-2 digital recorder with Sennheiser microphone and Telinga pro 22" parabolic reflector.

Habitat: Deciduous secondary forest with abundant Mountain Laurel undergrowth. Behavior: Perched 20 ft up in Red Oak just above dense Mountain Laurel giving several songs, eating caterpillars, and preening. Song frequency is approximately that which is heard in recording, so maybe once in every 10 seconds. Plumage: Adult male. Conditions: Moderate wind from south (probably the cause of this overshoot), partly cloudy, 75 F. Afternoon,

title: XC372592 Hooded Warbler (Setophaga citrina)
location: Colorado (near  Lakewood), Jefferson County, Colorado
description: Bird was singing spontaneously when we arrived, after playing the call note the bird popped into view, still singing it's A2 song.  "I wanna rent a video"!  The bird was deep in a dense thicket, popping up once or twice and birders snapped some pictures.  I took a short video and extracted the song clip from a video that contained people talking in front and after the song.  No other editing was done other than trimming down the movie file and then converting to mp3.  This bird is a rare vagrant to this area, usually a few are seen every year, so more uncommon than rare would maybe be more accurate. The bird continued to sing for some time during this day.  The bird was only seen this day and the day before at this location.
author: Dean Shoup

title: XC307684 House Finch (Haemorhous mexicanus)
location: Oxford, Lafayette County, Mississippi
description:
Natural sound. Several individuals foraging in three isolated mature pine trees.

#Habitat#
State waterfowl refuge along the margins of USACE flood control reservoir. Strip along the lake margins ~1km wide of moist soil grassland with mix of forbs, native warm season grasses (Andropogon, Schyzachyrium, Eragrostis, Aristida, etc.), and some sparse woody vegetation (Cephalanthus, Quercus saplings, etc.) bounded by oak hickory forest and, in places, pine plantation.  Three or four shallow waterfowl impoundments partially flooded in the winter.

#Editing#
No edits

#Equipment#
Fostex FR-2 digital recorder with Sennheiser microphone and Telinga pro 22" parabolic reflector.
author: J.R. Rigby
