title: XC441749 House Sparrow (Passer domesticus)
location: Inishbofin, Galway, County Galway
description: The clip records a flush of House Sparrows brought about by a false alarm. This, of course, is a regular occurrence among all birds that face the risk of predation constantly. The false alarm was caused by the sudden appearance of a group of wild Rock Doves that flew over a feeding area used by House Sparrows, Starlings and, indeed, the Rock Doves themselves. Hence their arrival in itself caused the smaller birds to react. Not all the House Sparrows fled. Some dived into bushes. Soon all were back out in the open and feeding - as though nothing had happened. The recording opens with calls from a Robin at 0:02 and 0:04; then the Robin broadcasts a series of ticking notes at 0:07 until the end of the ninth second. At 0:15 a Blackbird alarms but, just before that, the first wave of House Sparrows erupt into flight at 0:12.  By 0:15 the remainder explode. By the sixteenth second, a total of 80 House Sparrows have left the ground. Those that did not fly away completely (but are still within the bush) start to 'dust themselves down' and are calling. House Sparrows use a 'meep' call when they are agitated. Often it is doubled into a fast repeat that reminds me of the 'meep meep' of the Roadrunner cartoon bird. Especially from 0:18, a chorus of meep notes can be heard.  Although they are not 'doubled up' on this clip, under other circumstances when just one individual becomes uneasy, it frequently cries wolf with a 'meep meep' that serves as a clarion red alert to all that hear it. In fact, not just House Sparrows react to the signal - but  other birds too.
author: Anthony McGeehan

title: XC263718 House Wren (Troglodytes aedon)
location: Prairieville (near  Delton), Barry County, Michigan
description:
Clipped and cleaned segment from XC263717, example of female house wren song.  Background noise filtered out.

Recording made after a female playback trial (~5min after).  Female and male identified with unique leg band colors by an observer several meters away.  Several copulation solicitations and successful copulations observed before recording started.  Female leaned over and fluttered during many songs in this recording.  Male and female in close proximity throughout.  Weather sunny in the 70s.  Recorded on the day of the female's 3rd egg.  Female 3 years old.
XC290436 is a recording from the same female a year earlier.

location: Wright Creek, Prince George, British Columbia
description:
- four songs by same adult male.
- extraneous sounds edited by silencing rather than cutting out to preserve time interval between songs.
- bird singing from mixed forest edge about 5 meters up a Trembling Aspen.
- habitat is grass pastures with fields separated by blocks of mixed conifer (spruce/fir/pine) and deciduous (trembling aspen/cottonwood) forest; forest floor with medium understorey of thimbleberry, saskatoon, and rose; forest edge shrubs and vegetation include willows, rose, saskatoon, common cow-parsnip.
- UTM coordinates from Google Earth: Zone 10U 518349.04 E, 5996841.67 N (WGS84) 
- Lazuli Bunting has been pushing rapidly northward in central BC the past decade and has become established as a breeder in the Prince George area over the past three years. 
- this recording is an attempt to document the main song variant used by these northern vanguard breeders.
- recording device: H2 Zoom.
- sound editing done in Audacity.
- recording available in WAV format upon email request.
background: Swainson's Thrush (Catharus ustulatus); Olive-sided Flycatcher (Contopus cooperi); Ruby-crowned Kinglet (Regulus calendula); MacGillivray's Warbler (Geothlypis tolmiei)

secondary_labels: ['Pheucticus melanocephalus_Black-headed Grosbeak', 'Geothlypis trichas_Common Yellowthroat', 'Pipilo maculatus_Spotted Towhee', 'Turdus migratorius_American Robin', 'Piranga ludoviciana_Western Tanager', 'Melospiza melodia_Song Sparrow', 'Zonotrichia leucophrys_White-crowned Sparrow']
location: Private Property near Chehalis, Lewis County, Washington
description: One pure, brightly-plumaged male singing from a low power line about 4-5 meters off the ground, photographs taken. Power lines were built over a prominent hill with a stream running below and to the right of the singing bird. Clear-cut field behind the bird, pastureland in front, with a few scattered deciduous trees. This individual had been singing from the very top dead twigs of a 13-18 meter lone deciduous tree between the clear-cut and the pastures. It left the tree twice while I was watching it, but returned several minutes later and continued singing each time. It then flew to the power line above and in front of me, and I began recording 10 meters away from it. Weather conditions: the sun had just set, a few scattered high clouds, no wind, warm temperatures. This individual had been seen drinking/bathing in a small stream several hours previously far away from its preferred singing perch, across the pastures. No other individuals have been located in this area. Heavy interference at end of recording caused by the power lines. Oh, and the “screams” after 1:00 were from goats/sheep.
background: Black-headed Grosbeak (Pheucticus melanocephalus); Common Yellowthroat (Geothlypis trichas); Spotted Towhee (Pipilo maculatus); American Robin (Turdus migratorius); Western Tanager (Piranga ludoviciana); Song Sparrow (Melospiza melodia); White-crowned Sparrow (Zonotrichia leucophrys)

I could hear the bird moving around so I knew it was in there and then it started making this vocalization when I was about 15 ft away.  I had never heard a LEBI do this before so I thought there might also be a CLRA in there.  I played the similar CLRA call and this bird responded immediately, making me think there was indeed a CLRA nearby. title: XC322813 Least Bittern (Ixobrychus exilis)
secondary_labels: ['Quiscalus mexicanus_Great-tailed Grackle', 'Pipilo maculatus_Spotted Towhee', "Calypte anna_Anna's Hummingbird"]
location: Santee, San Diego County, California
description: I did not hear the sound right away due to the high vocal activity from the other birds and sound pollution from the plane and other patrons at the park.  However, I picked out something out of place in the first patch of reeds at the southwest end of Lake #6.  My first thought was Pied-billed Grebes- which I had seen at previous lakes, but not at this one.  Additionally, the Pied-billed Grebes were calling throughout the day, so I got a good refresher as to what they are supposed to sound like.  Since this sound was non-variable, low in pitch, and only used four notes that did not change in volume or pitch, my second guess was Least Bittern since they are known to make "coo" sounds four to five times.  However, since I could not see nor call out the bird, and the sound was also not very clear or loud, I did not publish the sound right away since I was not certain.  Subsequent analysis by ornithology professor Dr. Kevin Burns of San Diego State University, and avid birdwatcher Matt Sadowski convinced me this was the bird I suspected.  The calls can be hear at approximately 0:02, 0:09, 0:16, and 0:28.
background: Great-tailed Grackle (Quiscalus mexicanus); Spotted Towhee (Pipilo maculatus); Anna's Hummingbird (Calypte anna)
author: Joshua Jaeger

When called with a Scarlet Tanager chip the bird came down into bushes in front of me about 10ft and chipped at me.  I thing this was an female Scarlet Tanager.

I'm also curious what you think the vireo singing at the end it.  I think it is a yellow-throated vireo.

Thanks,
Gary

title: XC398858 LeConte's Thrasher (Toxostoma lecontei)
location: Joshua Tree, San Bernardino County, California
description: The bird was seen sitting at the top top of a 4-5 ft. tall creosote bush (Larrea tridentata) and was singing. The bird was a medium-sized thrasher, slightly smaller than a mockingbird and was a plain, drab, sandy gray color. I could make out the cinnamon/buffy color on the undertail coverts of the bird as well as the dark black eyes and noticeably decurved black bill. I was able to obtain diagnostic photographs although the light was getting low at that time of the day. I am not sure of the age or sex of the bird other than it was an adult. The bird was looking around as it sang and eventually ran rapidly on the ground and was lost from sight. I was able to relocate the bird 50 yards from the original sighting location (~30 yards from where I was now standing), on the top of a ranch-type wooden signpost approximately 6-7 ft. off the ground. A this point is when I took a recording using my iPhone. The bird was singing form this perch as the sun was setting, and flew off after approximately 3 minutes of song.
author: Derek Lecy

location: Oxford, Lafayette County, Mississippi
description:
Natural sound. Flushed from grass onto partridgepea and then into small sapling ~10m away. Issued two high buzzy calls before flying away.

#Habitat#
State waterfowl refuge along the margins of USACE flood control reservoir. Strip along the lake margins ~1km wide of moist soil grassland with mix of forbs, native warm season grasses (Andropogon, Schyzachyrium, Eragrostis, Aristida, etc.), and some sparse woody vegetation (Cephalanthus, Quercus saplings, etc.) bounded by oak hickory forest and, in places, pine plantation.  Three or four shallow waterfowl impoundments partially flooded in the winter.

#Editing#
Edited in Adobe Audition. Butterworth high-pass filter, order 3, cutoff frequency 1kHz

#Equipment#
Fostex FR-2 digital recorder with Sennheiser microphone and Telinga pro 22" parabolic reflector.

title: XC179344 Long-billed Curlew (Numenius americanus)
location: Las Animas CR 223 south of US-160, Las Animas Co., Colorado
description: natural vocalizations.  In this cut two adult birds are having a violent dispute, fighting and beating at each other with their wings while on the ground.  Mid-way through the cut both birds fly off in opposite directions.  I kept the mic on one of them, which gave some different call types for the rest of the cut.  Habitat was an open grassy pasture with no shrubs of any kind, but most of the surrounding grassland had a high density of sandsage and yucca.
author: Andrew Spencer

title: XC179483 Long-billed Curlew (Numenius americanus)
location: Comanche National Grassland - North Fork allotment, Baca Co., Colorado
description: natural vocalization; song during a flight display by a male bird.  During the display the bird would fly with rapid wingbeats to about 10m off the ground and then vocalize as it slowly descended, with the rapid trill as it reached the bottom of the flight about 1-2m off the ground before rising again to repeat. While giving the display the bird would travel in a large circle over the grassland.  Habitat was shortgrass prairie with very few shrubs.
author: Andrew Spencer

title: XC179484 Long-billed Curlew (Numenius americanus)
location: Comanche National Grassland - North Fork allotment, Baca Co., Colorado
description: natural vocalization; song from the same bird as in XC179483.  An especially long song bout from this bird.  While making this recording I was near one edge of the bird's prolonged aerial circuit, so most of the song is distant, but towards the end of the cut the bird flew very close overhead.  The harsh call at 2:24 was given at the closest point of the display to where I was standing and may be a reaction to my presence.  The trill at the end of the cut is given as the bird landed at the end of the display flight.
author: Andrew Spencer

title: XC313904 Louisiana Waterthrush (Parkesia motacilla)
location: Townsend, Blount County, Tennessee
description:
I need the "spectrum experts" for this one.  :-)

I saw a waterthrush perch in low shrubs near the slow-moving stream and it appeared to be NOWA, by underside coloration, in the brief glimpse I had.  

Seconds later, in the stream at that location, I saw two waterthrushes foraging, but did not get a great view.  Shortly, they took off and chased each other around and through the rhododendrons, "chinking" and chattering.  That's what is recorded here.

Are there two waterthrush species here?  The "chinks" at, for instance, 23.5-24.2 secs are a different frequency than those, say, at 18.5-20.5 secs.



playback-used:no
background: Swainson's Warbler (Limnothlypis swainsonii); Hooded Warbler (Setophaga citrina)

title: XC332613 Magnolia Warbler (Setophaga magnolia)
location: Lunenburg (near  Auburndale), Lunenburg County, Nova Scotia
description:
This recording was originally posted as a mystery recording. With the help of Paul Driver it was identified as a fledgling Magnolia Warbler. 

This species is a breeding bird at this site, and though my view was limited, the yellow belly also pointed to this i.d.

(Original notes: 
Morning, warm, in a field growing up in birch and pine, at edge of mixed deciduous/hemlock forest. Bird was a warbler and had a yellow belly which seemed to extend to the tail--though I am not certain on this. It looked to have a dark undertail, and back was gray, which may or may not include the head--the bird was screened by branches which made it difficult to really get a good look or a photo. The call was a note repeated three times in quick succession. You can hear it in response to my pishing. There are also sounds of chickens in background, and of a squirrel.)

title: XC396201 Marsh Wren (Cistothorus palustris)
location: Ellensburg, Kittitas County, Washington
description: The recording was high-pass filtered at 3000 Hz with a roll-off of 12 dB/Hz to eliminate road noise. The bird was perched on a barbed wire fence and was calling in response to aggression from another bird. The other bird was only seen poorly and could have been another Marsh Wren. The bird calling in this recording was moving away from me as time progressed, so later calls are from farther away. This call appears to be the kek-call. It's unknown whether subspecies in Kittitas county are C. p. pulverius or browningi/paludicola, particularly individuals found during the Winter. The only other species present were Song Sparrow and Fox Sparrow (XC396200). Recording made on an handheld Olympus LS-10 linear PCM recorder.

title: XC399844 Mountain Chickadee (Poecile gambeli)
location: Pocatello, Bannock County, Idaho
description:
This recording was not modified. It was chilly with clear skies and light breeze. About 6-24 inches of snow on the ground, varying depending on specific location. The habitat was semi-open sagebrush and Douglas fir dominated slopes. I heard a single chickadee performing short, high-pitched whistles. I pished briefly ~3 seconds, and the bird almost immediately came in and vocalized excitedly and gradually moved back in the firs, returning to general calls. I recorded when the bird came in and as it moved back into the firs. This bird was a classic adult Mountain Chickadee.

The bird was in the upper quarter of the Douglas firs foraging and calling. After I pished, it came in to as low as eye level and moved in the trees fluctuating between upper and mid levels of the trees after that. It called and flitted excitedly for a couple minutes and gradually moved back to foraging.
author: Austin Young

description:
Flew up from a privet hedge as I walked up. Landed within 5m of me and repeated the common call note for over a minute until I walked on.

# Habitat #
29-acre estate centrally located in Oxford, MS consisting of antebellum home surrounded by lawns and adjacent forest. Privet hedges and small thickets divide the grounds into distinct lawn units. Bordered on all sides by mature oak-hickory forest. Forest edge consists of oak spp, hickory spp, red cedar, mulberry, with understory along the edge dominated by privet (Ligustrum sp.). Grounds around the house include isolated trees and manicured hedges. A path from the end of the parking area leads northward ~1 km through the forest to the northern edge of the property abutting the University of Mississippi campus.

# Editing #
Audacity high-pass filter with 6 dB rolloff at 2 kHz

title: XC290060 Northern Harrier (Circus hudsonius)
location: Oxford, Lafayette County, Mississippi
description:
Two Northern Harriers, both in female/juvenile type plumage, flew in while I was audio recording a Sedge Wren and hunted intensively for a few moments with feet dangling below them as they coursed over the grass. One of the birds vocalized as it dived into the grass. The second bird responded vocally with a variant call and then flew over and joined its companion on the ground. About five minutes later both birds took off, flying together purposefully to the west and climbing higher and higher as they went. I was unable to age the two birds properly because of the low-angle light and distance while holding the microphone. The whole interaction struck me as a parent hunting with a juvenile. 

#Habitat#
State waterfowl refuge along the margins of USACE flood control reservoir. Strip along the lake margins ~1km wide of moist soil grassland with mix of forbs, native warm season grasses (Andropogon, Schyzachyrium, Eragrostis, Aristida, etc.), and some sparse woody vegetation (Cephalanthus, Quercus saplings, etc.) bounded by oak hickory forest and, in places, pine plantation.  Three or four shallow waterfowl impoundments partially flooded in the winter.

#Editing#
Edited in Adobe Audition. Butterworth high-pass filter, order 3, cutoff frequency 1kHz. Cut from the same recording as XC290059.

#Equipment#
Fostex FR-2 digital recorder with Sennheiser microphone and Telinga pro 22" parabolic reflector.
background: Swamp Sparrow (Melospiza georgiana); Song Sparrow (Melospiza melodia)
author: J.R. Rigby

title: XC316441 Northern Parula (Setophaga americana)
location: Oxford, Lafayette County, Mississippi
description:
Natural sound. Bird singing from midway up a large Southern Red Oak tree. 

#Habitat#
29-acre estate centrally located in Oxford, MS consisting of antebellum home surrounded by lawns and adjacent forest. Privet hedges and small thickets divide the grounds into distinct lawn units. Bordered on all sides by mature oak-hickory forest. Forest edge consists of oak spp, hickory spp, red cedar, mulberry, with understory along the edge dominated by privet (Ligustrum sp.). Grounds around the house include isolated trees and manicured hedges. A path from the end of the parking area leads northward ~1 km through the forest to the northern edge of the property abutting the University of Mississippi campus

#Editing#
Edited in Adobe Audition. Butterworth high-pass filter, order 3, cutoff frequency 800 Hz

#Equipment#
Fostex FR-2 digital recorder with Sennheiser microphone and Telinga pro 22" parabolic reflector.

Although all of these features can be variable and not always easy to see except under ideal conditions. The bird was in a shrub in the shade of the forest understory. Recording to my ear isn't diagnostic but I don't have a ton of experience with either bird. title: XC313284 Northern Rough-winged Swallow (Stelgidopteryx serripennis)
location: Arcata, Humboldt County, California
description:
This 10 second recording exhibits 4 quiet and subtle vocalizations of a perched Northern Rough-winged Swallow. Sex of the vocalist was not determined. The age of this vocalist was an after hatch year. The first vocalization is like the two-click ending to the following 3 calls. The last 3 calls were a down slurred 'eeoooo' following by 2-3 clicks. The eeoooo sound is reminiscent of a Cliff Swallow song. My attention was drawn to this bird when it uttered the several typical "brritt" calls while perched. But eventually I realized it was also giving this call type. It gave perhaps two bouts of this over a minute or two before I positioned myself to record this video. I then continued to watch this bird for a couple more minutes while it gave 3-5 calls with a long silent break between bouts. This bird was eventually flushed by a passing truck.

More details of the context of this recording may be found here: <http://ebird.org/ebird/view/checklist?subID=S29106888>
This recording was made with an Canon 7D Mark II camera with built-in mike. This is an unedited and unmodified recording of the natural spacing of this bird’s utterances.

There is a bit of wind noise.
author: Elias Aristides Elias

description:
Walking up Vista Del Lago to its highest point in Mission Viejo, CA.  As I approached the crest of the hill I heard a high pitched continuous alarm type call but was unable to ID initially.   As I followed the call I noted a woodpecker hole in a slightly decaying tree.  Sure enough the chick(s) were in the woodpecker tree hollow.  Now, how does one ID the bird?  I waited until the parent arrived and confirmed by sight and call it was a Nuttall's Woodpecker.

The recording starts with presumed male flying high over presumed female in nest. It was calling in a flight display carrying what appeared to be a clump of grass.  The grass looks similar to a fish and a Bald Eagle was following closely.

The presumed male then flew and called much closer to nest, follow by a dive at 1:26 towards the nest with female. The male continued to call.  The female finally responded with some calls.  The male called more and then dove (at 3:03) towards and landed on the nest at 3:08.  A least one of them called some more from the nest, with a few more Ospreys calling in background that were attracted to the activities.

title: XC298777 Ovenbird (Seiurus aurocapilla)
location: Division No. 4, Subd. A (near  La Poile), Division No. 4, Newfoundland and Labrador
description:
This is an interesting recording from the Starlight Trail, in the Table Mountains of southwestern Newfoundland. The persistent chip calls and occasional bouts of song are being given by adult Ovenbirds, of which there were four present during the observation. I was sitting on the ground for a better vantage, and the action was happening in the adjacent undergrowth. The adults were displacing each other and chasing each other around. There was one fledgling present, which was remaining motionless and silent.

Remarkably, this appears to be the first recording of this species from the island of Newfoundland in the xeno-canto archive.
author: Matthew Halley

State waterfowl refuge along the margins of USACE flood control reservoir. Three or four shallow waterfowl impoundments partially flooded in the winter.

title: XC183609 Pacific-slope Flycatcher (Empidonax difficilis)
location: Sequoia National Forest, Tulare County, California
description:
This bird was singing from a red fir forest at 9200 feet ASL. Position notes seemed similar to Cordilleran Flycatcher. But this flycatcher was not expected in the county. I put the only two position notes that I was able to record back to back at the beginning of this recording. The remainder of the recording is of the best signals of the dawn song that I was able to get in the 12 minute recording. 

Using this webpage: (<http://www.appliedbioacoustics.com/research/wefl/frameindex.html>) I was able to determine that this bird showed vocal characteristics of both Cordilleran and Pacific-slope Flycatchers. The "male position note" was distinctly two parted like a COFL yet was about 1 kHZ higher than a COFL ought to be. Phrase 1 of the dawn song was right at 6 kHz or right in the middle of where COFL and PSFL ought to be. Phrase 2 was shaped like a PSFL Phrase 2 and finally Phrase 3 was shaped like a PSFL Phrase 3.

some more details may be found here: <http://ebird.org/ebird/view/checklist?subID=S18918255>

Not much can be told with spending only 14 minutes with a bird, but this bird appeared to be a desperate male who was traveling and singing across the landscape hoping to get within earshot of a receptive female. It would spend a minute or two singing and then fly 100-150m to the next songpost and I chased it trying to get a better recording twice before finally giving up. At that point it had traveled approx 350 meters to the northwest from where I initially encountered the bird.
background: Hermit Thrush (Catharus guttatus); Audubon's Warbler (Setophaga auduboni)
author: Elias Aristides Elias

title: XC188559 Pectoral Sandpiper (Calidris melanotos)
location: Ikroavik Lake, Barrow, North Slope Borough, Alaska
description: natural vocalizations; calls from several birds both perched and in flight on somewhat wet tundra that had many drier patches interspersed.  The initial series of bubbly chase calls are from three different males chasing each other, with a female bird giving the loud trill call.  The subsequent raspy calls are from the female bird on the ground, appearing to be performing a distraction display running hunkered down through the grass with its rump exposed and tail flared.  The low pitched gurgle and then hooting song that follow are from one of the previous males in flight, returning from the chase.  The female then does more of her raspy calls before the singing male starts a tail-cocked display while running on the ground after the female and giving the series of lower-pitched raspy calls.  The male bird then breaks into (at 0:40) an alternating series of fast, modulated low-pitched hoots and higher pitched, mechanical sounding, rising/falling trills while the female gives the louder modulated calls.  In short, a remarkable variety of displays and calls all in about a minute!
author: Andrew Spencer

title: XC181947 Phainopepla (Phainopepla nitens)
location: Klamath County, Oregon
description: adult male Phainopepla, first known occurance in Klamath County, Oregon. First heard while conducting point count survey. I did not see the bird. Returned approx. one-half hour later and saw the bird atop a large yellow-flowering elderberry bush/small tree. It was preening and seemingly easily approachable. I took photos at first. Returned with fLIP camera and made one recording. I observed at close range its black plumage, crest, and red irises. An Anna's Hummingbird vocalized nearby. The habitat was an open large Oregon White Oak and grass area with pioneering Western Juniper which still left the area open. I did not note the smaller brush. It preferred the elderberry, but rested atop most prominent tops of small to medium sized bushes, shrubs, and trees.  It vocalized quite often, and seemed to have the same amount of time vocalizing as periods of silence. It did not sing, but its vocals were only the single note whistles as heard on this recording. I was in the vicinity a total of about 45 minutes including the point count time and relocating effort time.
background: Anna's Hummingbird (Calypte anna)

title: XC320703 Pileated Woodpecker (Dryocopus pileatus)
location: Burma Drive, Nanaimo, British Columbia
description:
The recording was extracted from the last 6 minutes of a 59 minute video taken with my camera, a Panasonic FZ200, with an added external Sennheiser MKE 400 microphone set up on a tripod in the parking area of the entrance to Linley Valley (Coddle Lake) Park at the end of Burma Road in Nanaimo, BC. A PIWO nest that had been discovered nine days earlier on May 29 still had two nestlings. Adults returned to feed the nestlings roughly every hour. While waiting, the nestlings were generally quiet. The nest was about 5 meters up in a large snag about 1 meter from the top and about 10 meters from the parking area.

The recording starts with both nestlings sticking their heads out of the nest waiting. At 0:05 a male adult arrives at the nest. One nestlings starts begging while the other gives out a short adult-like call and gets the first meal, regurgitated by the adult, at 00:07. That nestling proceeds to disappear into the nest leaving the other nestling alone to beg to the adult. At 0:12 this second nestling gets its first meal. At 0:19 this nestling gets a second meal. After poking at the adult the nestling gets a third course at 0:33 and a fourth at 0:43. Subsequent attempts to poke the adult for more fail and the adult just hangs on the tree as if waiting for something for 4 more minutes during which time the nestling begs continuously. Finally, the adult leaves after nearly 5 minutes at the nest. A few seconds later at 5:33 a drumming sound is heard, presumably by the adult, and both nestling heads appear outside the nest. The first nestling makes a couple more adult like calls at 5:40 and the camera battery dies shortly thereafter ending the recording.

The recording will end up online eventually and I will provide a link here.
author: Kevin Hood

location: Maple Leaf, Seattle, King County, Washington
description:
2 birds in this recording, one on a telephone pole, the louder of the two, and one in the distance who is both drumming and calling. The bird on the pole would drum, then stop and listen for the second bird. I've heard a single bird drumming for over a month at this location, but this was the first time I heard 2 interacting.  In the end the bird on the pole flew off in the direction of the second bird.
I condensed this recording  (it was originally over 11 minutes long) and amplified it a bit so the second bird was easier to hear.

title: XC215459 Pinyon Jay (Gymnorhinus cyanocephalus)
location: Mono Mills, Inyo National Forest, Mono County, California
type: and what I call the "chuckle" at 0:36, call, trills, typical calls
description:
flock of about 300 feeding in Jefferey Pine forest. Birds often feeding on the ground. I often hear these trills in local flocks in fall/winter, though have not heard them represented in online libraries.
Individual jays giving these twitter calls often create more to respond in twitters. 
No editing done here except slight amplification
author: Kristie Nelson

title: XC215461 Pinyon Jay (Gymnorhinus cyanocephalus)
location: Mono Mills, Inyo National Forest, Mono County, California
type: also apparent contact calls (nasal), call, chorus of trills
description:
Flock of about 300 foraging in Jeffery Pine forest. Cut the sound of an overhead jet, but it was below the frequencies of the jay calls, also amplified the sound a little.
This is a nice example of the trill calls being uttered by many birds; it seems like sometimes one or a few start this call, and many in the flock respond (like this). I have not previously heard these trill calls from PIJAs in online sources, but I hear it frequently. There are several versions of trill calls given by birds in fall/winter -- high thin ones, low harsh ones.
This recording also has what I interpret to be contact calls -- short, quite nasal calls (reminiscent of Acorn Woodpecker) - also a call not found previously (by me at least) by this species.
author: Kristie Nelson

title: XC481942 Purple Finch (Haemorhous purpureus)
location: Ellensburg, Kittitas County, Washington
description: Natural song from a male Haemorhous finch. Given the unusual song type and proximity to previous recording, likely the same individual as XC472344. The chest streaking and extent of coloration suggest Purple Finch (Haemorhous pupureus), however, the coloration was orange-yellow rather than raspberry red. Purple Finch is unusual at this location during the summer. This individual was actively singing until well past 2PM in 80F weather and chasing away other House Finches (Haemorhous mexicanus) as if it were on territory. This recording was made a on an iPhone 6 and extracted from a video recording.
author: Walter Szeliga

title: XC488611 Purple Finch (Haemorhous purpureus)
location: Vancouver Island (near  Oliver Woods Centre Pond), Nanaimo, British Columbia
description:
The Purple Finch song is intermixed with Towhee and other calls.  The first few Purple Finch songs are at 0:03, 0:09, 0:15, 0:22, ...
 
The bird was moving through the mid-story of some mixed conifer/deciduous along the edge of the pond.  It was singing a 2 second song/call about once every 4 to 5 seconds.  I compared the song with a number of xeon-canto Purple Finch recordings in the Victoria area (XC160261, XC160004, XC97639, XC160212, XC160217) and it does appear to be the song of a Purple Finch.

The [eBird checklist](https://ebird.org/view/checklist/S58349483) includes some images showing what looks like a female or juvenile Purple Finch.  Do female or hatch-year birds sing?

location: Big Bay State Park, Ashland, Wisconsin
description:
Two segments from a pair of birds.  It's unclear whether the calls were from the male or the female or both.  In the first segment, there were several calls in flight before landing about 20m from where I stood along the shore of the lagoon. After landing, they swam slowly toward me and watched me from a distance of 5-10m for about 15 minutes.  The second segment is the same pair calling as they flushed from the water and flew away.

Recorded with internal microphones of Olympus LS-10S.
background: Common Loon (Gavia immer); Alder Flycatcher (Empidonax alnorum); Common Yellowthroat (Geothlypis trichas); American Crow (Corvus brachyrhynchos); Song Sparrow (Melospiza melodia)

title: XC138945 Red-breasted Sapsucker (Sphyrapicus ruber)
location: Salt Spring Island, Capital, British Columbia
description:
Recording of a nestling Red-breasted Sapsucker.  The weather was clear, sunny and warm.  An adult returned to the nest roughly every 2 minutes to feed the young from outside the nest.  At least one nestling called continuously except during the second or so while they were being fed by an adult.  Adult visits at the nest were short - roughly 3 seconds in length.  The nestling's noisy response and brief quiet period can be heard starting just after 1:45 in the recording.

The nest was in a tree alongside a town street and not far from a relatively major road.

This recording was made using an iPhone 4.  It was normalized and high-pass filtered with cutoff at 1500 Hz and a rolloff of 24 db per octave to remove wind and street noise.

See also:
ML89586 - similar recording of nestlings (2:22)
ML169749 - similar nestling begging (40s)
ML47586 - adults and nestlings (younger since adults still entering nest to feed)

State waterfowl refuge along the margins of USACE flood control reservoir. Three or four shallow waterfowl impoundments partially flooded in the winter.

Edited in Adobe Audition. Butterworth high-pass filter, order 3, cutoff frequency 1 kHz

Fostex FR-2 digital recorder with Sennheiser microphone and Telinga pro 22" parabolic reflector.

title: XC113900 Red Crossbill (Loxia curvirostra)
location: Warszawa (near  Warsaw), Warszawa, Mazowieckie
description:
Flock abot 26 birds; composing 3 types of call - 2 not reported by work of Magnus S Robb - 
most of birds has similar calls for western dark Siberian taiga some similar to reported from eastern dark Siberian taiga and:

- call like in   0:00.715 is not reported by Magnus S. Robb. but has some similarities also in excitement call to type "F" (I have named it "Western Scotch Pine cohort")  - So I have named it as "Fe" with name - "Eastern Scotch Pine cohort" (named in XC sometimes as x) - this birds are also very similar to "Siberian Pine cohort" or it is the same wandering throughout continent depending on "fertile years" of Norway and Siberian Spruce 

- call like in   0:03.257 is similar to reported C type call but with usual for continental spruce cohort spearheaded and bent right arm - more prominent like in "Cd" type soo I mark it as "Cf" call and named "Northern Spruce cohort" - placed east of "Scandinavian Spruce cohort" this birds are very similar to "Siberian Spruce cohort"  or it is the same wandering throughout continent depending on "fertile years" of Scotch and Siberian Pine

- cal on 0:00.643     0:03.883 is similar to "D" type reported in work of Magnus S Robb  and can belogns to unknown  Siberian Larch cohort

And excitement calls throughout the recording

Birds was feeding on Picea pungens with small cones similar to eastern Syberian Spruve - Picea obovata, rather omitting native Norway Spruce - Picea alba what can suggesting the origin of the bird flock rather form East Siberian cohorts
author: Jarek Matusiak

Singing bird belong to named "fe" type - not reported by Magnus S. Robb. but has some similarities also in excitement call to type "F" (I have named it "Western Scotch Pine cohort") - So I have named it as "Fe" with name - "Eastern Scotch Pine cohort" (named in XC sometimes as x - but prefer "fe" along the Magnus and beter finding results on WWW) - this birds are also very similar to "Siberian Pine cohort" or it is the same wandering throughout continent depending on "fertile years" of Norway and Siberian Spruce

title: XC290097 Red-tailed Hawk (Buteo jamaicensis)
location: Oxford, Lafayette County, Mississippi
description:
Soaring/hunting ~100ft above the ground overhead. Distance from microphone ~40m.

#Habitat#
State waterfowl refuge along the margins of USACE flood control reservoir. Strip along the lake margins ~1km wide of moist soil grassland with mix of forbs, native warm season grasses (Andropogon, Schyzachyrium, Eragrostis, Aristida, etc.), and some sparse woody vegetation (Cephalanthus, Quercus saplings, etc.) bounded by oak hickory forest and, in places, pine plantation.  Three or four shallow waterfowl impoundments partially flooded in the winter.

#Editing#
Edited in Adobe Audition. Butterworth high-pass filter, order 3, cutoff frequency 1 kHz

#Equipment#
Fostex FR-2 digital recorder with Sennheiser microphone and Telinga pro 22" parabolic reflector.
background: Song Sparrow (Melospiza melodia); Blue Jay (Cyanocitta cristata)

title: XC137659 Red-winged Blackbird (Agelaius phoeniceus)
location: Port Coquitlam, Greater Vancouver, British Columbia
type: begging call, flight call, juvenile, male, song
description:
Fledgling (begging and flight call) following adult 'babysitter' male (song).

The recording was taken near the marshy pond at the East edge of Colony Farm Regional Park.   The weather was sunny, warm (20 C) with little or no wind.  I was standing about 5 meters away from the two birds.

The adult male and a juvenile (fledgling) Red-winged Blackbird were perched on top of a 3m high bush.  The adult male sang occasionally (heard at 0:00, 0:13, 0:31 and 0:43) while the juvenile was continuously begging (with wing fluttering).  The juvenile calls were directed away from the adult suggesting that the adult male was not actively involved in feeding the young bird.   Towards the end of the recording the adult flew down into the bulrushes (the original nest site perhaps) at which point the juvenile immediately followed switching to a different 3-syllable 'wait for me' flight call which can be heard at 0:52, 0:54 and 0:56, getting fainter as the birds distanced themselves from their bush-top perch and the microphone.

I watched the male adult and juvenile move back and forth between the bulrushes and the bush-top at least twice during the time that I was there.

A picture of the fledgling is available here: <http://www.flickr.com/photos/94309556@N05/8965154915/>
author: KevinHHood

title: XC368057 Rock Wren (Salpinctes obsoletus)
location: Idaho (near  Blackfoot), Bonneville County, Idaho
description:
Edited: Using Raven Lite, I filtered out background noise (airplanes & highway) from above and below the Rock Wren call.

Habitat: lava fields, collapsed lava tubes, green rabbitbrush, wyoming sagebrush and utah juniper were the dominant shrub species. Forbs known included lomatium and primrose. 

Behavior: Actively foraging around a collapsed lava tube, darting in and out of broken lava rocks while calling. Occasionally took breaks to sing atop utah juniper, rocky outcrops, and dead snags. 

Plumage: Distant views, pale buffy front, deep knee-bends.

Sex: Unknown

Weather: Overcast and cool, very light precipitation for about 3 minutes.
background: American Robin (Turdus migratorius); Horned Lark (Eremophila alpestris)

No elements of the bird call were in this frequency band as confirmed by analyzing the spectrograph.  Also... it's a RCKI... they don't exactly do bass.

title: XC256200 Savannah Sparrow (Passerculus sandwichensis)
location: Ferndale, Humboldt County, California
description:
This 20 second recording documents 17 Alarm Calls of an adult Savannah Sparrow (likely male). This sparrow appeared to be threatened by my presence. The Bird of North American account says "1) Alarm call:  Emphatic broadband single note. Female usually a sharp, dry chip; male either a chip or more commonly a higher pitched tsip; pitch of alarm calls of both sexes increases in frequency with perceived danger of situation." Given this statement, this was likely a male because the spectrogram shows a nearby bird that was lower pitched was 180° off axis of the microphone.

More details of the context of this recording may be found here: <http://ebird.org/ebird/view/checklist?subID=S24205392>

This recording was made with an iPhone 4s with Sennheiser microphone and Røde Rec application. This is an unedited and unmodified cut of a longer 2 minute long recording of the natural spacing of this bird's utterances.
author: Elias Aristides Elias

Douglas-Fir, Lodgepole Pine forest, north-facing slope.
Species not confirmed at time of recording.
Returned to same location two days later (2017-05-06), and heard same call, and identified female SSHA.  Male flew joined her; they perched side-by-side briefly, then copulated.  Male flew off and gave typical SSHA call from a distance.  Female continued to give recorded call.  Both birds in adult plumage, though female eye-color was still yellow-orange.
SSHAs successfully nested nearby in 2014.

title: XC357958 Snow Goose (Anser caerulescens)
location: Sonny Bono Salton Sea National Wildlife Refuge, near Calipatria, Imperial County, California
description:
I was waiting for this moment since first seeing the large flocks of Snow Geese on this trip. I’d see them on land or in the water, occasionally taking off in flight. I was hoping a flock would fly directly over, allowing me to aim straight up to record, and they did this for me in this recording. Stereo would have been nice, but my stereo mics are omnidirectional and would have captured too much background noise. This recording was with one omni-mic and my 24 inch dish. 
    And I wish I had been able to video this spectacle: I expected an unorganized mob of geese, but they had not only arranged in their “V” formations already, but in multiple groups going in different directions at different heights above me. This created a spectacular geometric effect of moving quadrilaterals of blue sky boarderd by lines of white geese.
background: Gadwall (Mareca strepera); Song Sparrow (Melospiza melodia); Marsh Wren (Cistothorus palustris)
author: Thomas G. Graves

Fostex FR-2 digital recorder with Sennheiser microphone and Telinga pro 22" parabolic reflector.

title: XC287881 Song Sparrow (Melospiza melodia)
location: Oxford, Lafayette County, Mississippi
description:
Bird flushed from beneath an observation deck and into a thick patch of partridgepea (*Chamaecrista fasciculata*) approximately 5m away. Called repeatedly for ~30 sec and then disappeared into the dense vegetation.

# Habitat #
State waterfowl refuge along the margins of USACE flood control reservoir. Strip along the lake margins ~1km wide of moist soil grassland with mix of forbs, native warm season grasses (Andropogon, Schyzachyrium, Eragrostis, Aristida, etc.), and some sparse woody vegetation (Cephalanthus, Quercus saplings, etc.) bounded by oak hickory forest and, in places, pine plantation.  Three or four shallow waterfowl impoundments partially flooded in the winter.

# Editing #
No edits other than excerpting from longer recording.

title: XC288255 Song Sparrow (Melospiza melodia)
location: Oxford, Lafayette County, Mississippi
description:
Bird was perched 2-3 m above the ground near the top of an isolated box elder (Acer negundo) in an open grassland ~50m from a forest edge. I was only about 5-8 m from the bird and watched the bird through binoculars while recording because I could not see the bill opening. If the bill was opened at all, it was very slight, but the tail and plumage quivered during the vocalizations. Just after 1:34 a male Northern Cardinal chased the bird out of the tree briefly before the juvenile and a second Song Sparrow returned to chase away the Cardinal. After this the juvenile resumed singing while the second sparrow moved away into the grass. 

# Editing #
Adobe Audition FFT filter, 2048 pts, Blackman window, 1 kHz to 14 kHz bandpass.

title: XC174354 Sora (Porzana carolina)
location: Orlando Wetlands, Christmas, Orange County, Florida
description:
It was in marsh cattails with other Soras. I wasn't 100% positive of its ID when I heard it, but I presumed it was a Sora.

Similar to this: XC163779

and this: http://macaulaylibrary.org/audio/2864

There's a faint repetitive clacking call in background that is a Virginia Rail call.  Here is a better recording of the background bird originally uploaded as a mystery: XC174366.

*On March 22, 2015 a Sora made a couple of these call right in front of me at close range.  I was just watching the Sora and it just went barely out of sight into the marsh when I heard this call at its position.  It only made two calls.

Shortly after, a few meters deeper into the marsh, and out of sight, I heard this call 1/2 dozen more times.  I immediately saw movement of the vegetation go quickly two different directions.  I soon saw that one of the moving birds was a Sora and most likely both were Soras, as many were in the wetlands. 

I'm guessing Soras make this call in agitation, such as when one meets another unexpectedly.  Perhaps this bird is agitated by the Virginia Rail?

secondary_labels: ['Agelaius phoeniceus_Red-winged Blackbird', 'Colaptes auratus_Northern Flicker', 'Rallus limicola_Virginia Rail']
location: Los Alamos National Laboratory (near  Los Alamos), Los Alamos County, New Mexico
description:
This recording was made using the built-in microphone on my Motorola Nexus 6 mobile phone.   It has undergone slight amplification (+8dB) using Adobe Audition.  

I was standing about 4 meters from the bird while it was hiding in the reeds of the marshy area at the bottom of Sandia Canyon.  This area is on Los Alamos National Laboratory property and is off-limits to the general public.  After the recording was made, I played a sora "whinney" call using iBird and the bird walked out into the open to investigate for about five seconds, then returned to its hiding place and continued calling.  This call persisted for over five minutes.  

The high-pitched descending notes heard occasionally (first at 0:38) in the background was a Red-winged Blackbird perched at the top of a reed.  It also makes three of the nasal trill calls common to RWBB (first at 0:50).  Coincident with the first of these trill calls and in the background, you can hear a second more distant Sora making a whinney call.    At 1:11 a Northern Flicker drums on a distant snag.  At 1:42 a Virginia Rail makes a grunt call nearby.
background: Red-winged Blackbird (Agelaius phoeniceus); Northern Flicker (Colaptes auratus); Virginia Rail (Rallus limicola)
author: Mouser Williams

title: XC481855 Sora (Porzana carolina)
location: Eagle Creek Park,  Indianapolis, Marion County, Indiana
description:
Short, sharp calls believed to be the "keep" call of Kaufmann, G. W. (1983. Displays and vocalizations of the Sora and the Virginia Rail. Wilson Bulletin 95:42-59), which is presumably comparable to the abbreviated "kee" or "weep" call of BNA. Note, however, that, BNA attributes call to mating while Kauman states it is associated with hostility/alarm. 

My recording came from a bird that was seen well in sparse cattails approx five meters away. Although the bird was seen foraging, based on posture and movement, it appeared that the bird was agitated by a Northern Watersnake (Nerodia sipedon) that was within 0.5-2 meters of the bird. The snake was coiled and resting on dead cattails approx 20 cm above the water of the pond. Photo of the bird and snake are included with my eBird checklist with the submission ID of S55258823.
background: Red-winged Blackbird (Agelaius phoeniceus)

title: XC255373 Spotted Sandpiper (Actitis macularius)
location: Petrolia, Humboldt County, California
description:
This 11 second recording documents 14 alarm vocalizations of an adult Spotted Sandpiper. There appear to be two variants in this recording. The first type is a higher pitched squared-off note that peaks at approx 4.5kHz. The second type is a lower pitched smooth arch-shaped note which peaks at approx 3.5kHz. Both notes have a similarity to the call of a Pygmy Nuthatch. This vocalist was perched on driftwood on a beach. And was alert to and seemed agitated by my presence. There may have been eggs/young in the area but this bird did not perform a broken-wing act as I wandered around. However I did note a second Spotted Sandpiper silently scurry away. This is an unedited and unmodified recording of the natural spacing of this bird’s utterances.

This could be the call that the BNA calls the alarm call. The BNA account described it thus: Alarm Calls. Consist of weet weet and peet peet peet and are given on the ground or in flight. When flushed, typical call is an extended series of the same notes: tweet-weet-tweet-weet-weettweet-weet-weet-weet-weet (Smith 1914, Stone 1937, Knowles 1942). When alarmed by an intruder, call changes to metallic spink spink if chicks present (Stone 1937), a louder version of Pink Call (see below).

Additional details regarding context may be found at: <http://ebird.org/ebird/view/checklist?subID=S24148474>

This recording was made with an iPhone 5s with stock microphone and Røde Rec application.
author: Elias Aristides Elias

title: XC287880 Swamp Sparrow (Melospiza georgiana)
location: Oxford, Lafayette County, Mississippi
description:
High, buzzy "zheet" calls. Bird seen briefly as it flushed into the tall grass. Recorded while out of sight.

# Habitat #
State waterfowl refuge along the margins of USACE flood control reservoir. Strip along the lake margins ~1km wide of moist soil grassland with mix of forbs, native warm season grasses (Andropogon, Schyzachyrium, Eragrostis, Aristida, etc.), and some sparse woody vegetation (Cephalanthus, Quercus saplings, etc.) bounded by oak hickory forest and, in places, pine plantation.  Three or four shallow waterfowl impoundments partially flooded in the winter. **Precise habitat location** in dense Andropogon virginicus near the forest edge. 

# Editing #
No edits beyond excerpting from longer recording.
author: J.R. Rigby

title: XC316431 Swainson's Thrush (Catharus ustulatus)
location: Oxford, Lafayette County, Mississippi
description:
Natural sound. Birds perched 1-2m above the ground in a privet thicket along the edge of the grounds just behind a mulberry tree with ripe berries. One bird singing initially, but sounded as though a second joined in at times. 

#Habitat#
29-acre estate centrally located in Oxford, MS consisting of antebellum home surrounded by lawns and adjacent forest. Privet hedges and small thickets divide the grounds into distinct lawn units. Bordered on all sides by mature oak-hickory forest. Forest edge consists of oak spp, hickory spp, red cedar, mulberry, with understory along the edge dominated by privet (Ligustrum sp.). Grounds around the house include isolated trees and manicured hedges. A path from the end of the parking area leads northward ~1 km through the forest to the northern edge of the property abutting the University of Mississippi campus

#Editing#
Edited in Adobe Audition. Butterworth high-pass filter, order 3, cutoff frequency 2 kHz

#Equipment#
Fostex FR-2 digital recorder with Sennheiser microphone and Telinga pro 22" parabolic reflector.
author: J.R. Rigby

title: XC396845 Tundra Swan (Cygnus columbianus)
secondary_labels: ['Grus grus_Common Crane', 'Anthus pratensis_Meadow Pipit', 'Anthus spinoletta_Water Pipit']
location: Cloppenburg (near  Bösel), Niedersachsen
description:
A flock of purely Tundra swans coming in to their roost during the evening twilight. All members of the flock were visually identified. I followed the flock with a parabolic microphone as they flew by, over a landscape probably also used by whooper swans for roosting. Birds on the ground were hidden, so there might also be calls from whooper swans on the ground in the recording. At the end it can be heard how the tundra swans land on a water surface (the woosh of the water can be heard) on the other end of the area (invisible to the observer) and start social interactions.
The area is a turf mining complex beeing partly rewetted and renatured. The swans, bean geese and cranes use the water surfaces in the renaturing areas for roosting.
background: Common Crane (Grus grus); Meadow Pipit (Anthus pratensis); Water Pipit (Anthus spinoletta)
author: Raoul Kima

title: XC362634 Veery (Catharus fuscescens)
location: New York (near  Millbrook), Dutchess County, New York
description:
This original record was made by Wieteke A. Holthuijzen as part of a long-term study initiated and supervised by Dr. Kenneth A. Schmidt (Assistant Professor, Behavioral Ecology of Birds and Mammals, Texas Tech University) at the Cary Institute of Ecosystem Studies campus. This study focuses on Veeries (Catharus fuscescens), heterospecific eavesdropping, and predation risk. 

The vocalizing Veeries for this recording were not seen, as they were passively recorded during a playback experiment (to study the acoustic response of Veeries to the high "seet" alarm call from Tufted Titmice [Baeolophus bicolor]) during the dusk chorus. The recording of this particular Veery call was made during the playback experiment. Since this was a passive playback experiment (i.e. the recorder was not there as to avoid disturbing the avian chorus and an omnidirectional microphone was left to passively record the dusk chorus), plumage features of the vocalizing individuals cannot be provided. 

The habitat in which this vocalizing Veeries were recorded is a mixed oak forest, largely composed of second-growth oak (Quercus spp.) and maple (Acer spp.). No information is available regarding the birds’ position or distance from the microphone. No additional physical behavior is noted; no photographs were taken. This particular recording was not altered or filtered, but it was clipped from a longer (65-minute) recording as part of an experimental playback trial. 

The Veery call in this recording is described as the “Buerr” call, which is a short call that falls downward at a convex angle, varying between tonal and harsh notes, sometimes with harmonics (K. A. Schmidt unpubl. data; Heckscher 2007 [U call]). Two different vocalizing Veeries are heard in this recording, both vocalizing “Buerr” calls. Two other recordings of different Veery calls were made at this same location within 24 hours (XC362508, XC362509). Another individual Veery can be heard singing in the distant background in this recording as well.

This research was supported in part by a grant to K.A. Schmidt from the National Science Foundation (CAREER grant DEB 0746985).

References
Heckscher, C. M. 2007. Use of the Veery (Catharus fuscescens) call repertoire in vocal communication. Thesis. University of Delaware, Newark, Delaware, USA.
author: Wieteke A. Holthuijzen

This research was supported in part by a grant to K.A. Schmidt from the National Science Foundation (CAREER grant DEB 0746985).

secondary_labels: ['Passerculus sandwichensis_Savannah Sparrow', 'Buteo jamaicensis_Red-tailed Hawk', 'Contopus cooperi_Olive-sided Flycatcher']
location: Mima Mounds, Thurston County, Washington
description: So, this is the bird I have named Hopeful. He's been hanging out in this location for several years now, and as far as I have seen, he's the only Vesper Sparrow here. He's constantly surrounded instead by Savannah Sparrows, and I believe he has picked up some song elements from them over the years, and so he now sounds like this. Yes, he is a Vesper Sparrow. Well-documented by me and many others, photographed, etc. His song is just very strange. Hopeful has a specific territory in the mounds (accurate to the meter when we relocate him) that he returns to each year, and he sings his little heart out in it. (Male is assumed, since male and female Vespers are similar.) When singing, he goes to a prominent perch over the tallest grasses (small scrub brush, short deciduous tree seedlings, fenceposts, etc.) much like the Savannah Sparrows. He doesn't seem to associate with the Savannahs, and we have seen them in conflict before. Weather: cool (around 60 degrees F), mostly cloudy (but still bright), occasional winds but usually calm with gentle or no breeze. Light amplification, and high pass filter used to cut out worst of wind noise.
background: Savannah Sparrow (Passerculus sandwichensis); Red-tailed Hawk (Buteo jamaicensis); Olive-sided Flycatcher (Contopus cooperi)

title: XC255604 Violet-green Swallow (Tachycineta thalassina)
location: Arcata, Humboldt County, California
description:
This 1+ minute recording documents a flock of swallows swarming me. The primary vocalist was an adult female Violet-green Swallow. Also present was an adult male Violet-green Swallow and an adult Barn Swallow (sex not determined). Other swallows were present but were not focused on but I assume they were probably their youngsters. The female was protecting a juvenile Barn Swallow (which she fed) perched on the nest box that she had raised her young in. This juvenile was incapable of sustained flight and just was resting near the VGSW box. These parents were attempting to drive me away. The recording begins with a volley of notes from the female and she each time she approaches me throughout the recording she is stooping on me. She also spends some time just circling me and giving single more spaced calls. At 0:17 the male make a two phrase scratchy vocalization at the bottom of a dive directed at me. At 0:44 a Barn Swallow begins to make noise. At 0:48 a Barn Sallow begins to chase an adult Common Raven.

The Birds of North America account says this about the alarm call: “Alarm” call. No published description, but apparent alarm calls recorded by D. J. Borror in El Paso Co., CO, are shown in Fig. 3 . Also a “zwrack” call, similar to that of Purple Martin (Progne subis), used in high-intensity alarm situations (Brown 1983).

Additional details regarding context may be found at: <http://ebird.org/ebird/view/checklist?subID=S24178105>

This recording was made with an iPhone 4s with Sennheiser microphone and Røde Rec application.
background: Barn Swallow (Hirundo rustica)
author: Elias Aristides Elias

title: XC200968 White-breasted Nuthatch (Sitta carolinensis)
location: Boulder, Boulder County, Colorado
description: For quite some time (more than 10 years now, actually), the carolinensis subspecies of the White-breasted Nuthatch has been reported from the back end (the west end) of the Walden/Sawhill complex. I'm not aware that any recordings have been made of the bird or birds at the site, so here is my effort. This particular bird wasn't especially vocal, but its call notes were of the "yarnk" and "yarnk, yarnk" variety characteristic of carolinensis. Plumage and morphometric characters were consistent with carolinensis.

title: XC462023 White-breasted Nuthatch (Sitta carolinensis)
location: Acton Grade Rd, Madera County, California
description:
Besides the commonly-heard single soft contact calls, these two nuthatches were giving two and three-note calls (peer-peer, peer-peer-peer) that closely resemble the "keer" calls described by Pieplow (2017) for the eastern subspecies (S. c. carolinensis). He describes this as "infrequent, by both sexes in courtship and high excitement", which fits perfectly with the context I observed. Two birds interacting closely, then chasing each other with this call increasing in intensity during the chase. Its a call I have heard a few times from this Pacific subspecies, but never before managed to get a recording.

Pieplow describes the eastern subspecies' "keer" call as "seminasal" but in this case, I see no indication of nasal tone (just clear harmonics) and also sounded non-nasal to the ear.
author: Ed Pandolfino

title: XC184175 White-crowned Sparrow (Zonotrichia leucophrys)
location: FR-2061, Deschutes National Forest, Deschutes County, Oregon
description: Grabbed from video with Canon PowerShot SX50 HS, filtered and edited for handling noise and for a shorter interval with Audacity. This dialect is very different from the birds in the Willamette Valley to the coast, but it's an astonishingly close match to recordings from the Puget Sound area and Vancouver Island. Yellow bill, narrower white lateral head stripes, and pale gray lores and supraloral were obvious in the field. Oriantha does not occur anywhere near here, despite the range map here, which is incorrect. The tongue extending down from NE Oregon should stop east of Bend and Prineville (not connect to the Cascades) and then extend southward from there to connect to the north-central and northeastern California populations. And considering the dialect of this bird, there should be a narrow finger extending southward through the Washington and Oregon Cascades.
author: Richard Hoyer

Strip along the lake margins ~1km wide of moist soil grassland with mix of forbs, native warm season grasses (Andropogon, Schyzachyrium, Eragrostis, Aristida, etc.), and some sparse woody vegetation (Cephalanthus, Quercus saplings, etc.) bounded by oak hickory forest and, in places, pine plantation.  Three or four shallow waterfowl impoundments partially flooded in the winter.

#Editing#
Edited in Adobe Audition. Butterworth high-pass filter, order 3, cutoff frequency 700 Hz. 

#Equipment#
Fostex FR-2 digital recorder with Sennheiser microphone and Telinga pro 22" parabolic reflector.

title: XC486018 White-crowned Sparrow (Zonotrichia leucophrys)
location: Rainbow Park (near  Victoria), Capital, British Columbia
description: Begging calls from single juvenile.  I have been watching the nest: this juvenile left the nest about 8 days ago.  It lacks flight feathers and spends most of the time hiding under dense shrubs.  At the beginning of the recording, the juvenile calls occasionally while the adult feeds on the open grass 5 to 10 meters away.  Toward the last portion of the recording, the adult returns to the juvenile, at which point the juvenile calls continuously, the adult opens its mouth, and juvenile feeds.  Afterwards, the adult departs and the begging calls cease.  I used a moderate high pass filter at  4000 Hz to reduce noise from three floatplanes.

title: XC288986 White-throated Sparrow (Zonotrichia albicollis)
location: Oxford, Lafayette County, Mississippi
description:
Perched in partridgepea along the entrance road 0.5 m above the ground. Abnormally warm for this date, 77 F. Breezy, 5-10 mph NW. Distance from microphone ~5m. 

# Habitat #
State waterfowl refuge along the margins of USACE flood control reservoir. Strip along the lake margins ~1km wide of moist soil grassland with mix of forbs, native warm season grasses (Andropogon, Schyzachyrium, Eragrostis, Aristida, etc.), and some sparse woody vegetation (Cephalanthus, Quercus saplings, etc.) bounded by oak hickory forest and, in places, pine plantation.  Three or four shallow waterfowl impoundments partially flooded in the winter.

# Editing #
Adobe Audition. Butterworth high-pass filter, cutoff 500 hz, order 3

# Equipment #
Fostex FR-2 digital field recorder with Telinga Pro 22" parabolic reflector

secondary_labels: ['Dumetella carolinensis_Gray Catbird', 'Melanerpes carolinus_Red-bellied Woodpecker', 'Geothlypis trichas_Common Yellowthroat']
location: "The Annex" Homestead, Miami-Dade, Florida
description: This is a recording of multiple "whit" calls of a Willow Flycatcher. The recording was made using the "voice memo" app on an iPhone 4S. The recording was slightly amplified using Audacity but is otherwise unedited. This bird has been present for nearly two months at this location, which is quite unusual, especially since this species is rarely recorded in Florida. The habitat is dense tropical shrubby hammock along a canal and road edge adjacent to a large open field. The area is just outside of the main entrance to Everglades National Park. The bird spent most of its time calling from deep within cover 5-10 feet off the ground. It briefly flew across the road and perched in the open and called a few more times. Poor photos were obtained in the early morning light.
background: Grey Catbird (Dumetella carolinensis); Red-bellied Woodpecker (Melanerpes carolinus); Common Yellowthroat (Geothlypis trichas)
author: Graham Williams

title: XC178977 Willow Flycatcher (Empidonax traillii)

It is - to the best of my knowledge - the only regular breeding location of the species in the state of Georgia.  There were actually two birds singing.  The location is very near a main artery of traffic through the town of Blairsville, and my vantage point is the only approach. Consequently there was a lot of morning noise and the recording is highly modified to accentuate the flycatcher, including noise reduction and high-pass filtering as well as discarding some sounds within the recording which would alter any perceived cadence of intervals between songs.

secondary_labels: ['Setophaga magnolia_Magnolia Warbler', 'Thryothorus ludovicianus_Carolina Wren', 'Hylocichla mustelina_Wood Thrush']
location: Oxford, Lafayette County, Mississippi
description:
Natural sound. Bird foraging very actively, almost frenetic, in privet and lower branches of trees along the entrance path ~3-5m above the ground.

#Habitat#
29-acre estate centrally located in Oxford, MS consisting of antebellum home surrounded by lawns and adjacent forest. Privet hedges and small thickets divide the grounds into distinct lawn units. Bordered on all sides by mature oak-hickory forest. Forest edge consists of oak spp, hickory spp, red cedar, mulberry, with understory along the edge dominated by privet (Ligustrum sp.). Grounds around the house include isolated trees and manicured hedges. A path from the end of the parking area leads northward ~1 km through the forest to the northern edge of the property abutting the University of Mississippi campus

#Editing#
Edited in Adobe Audition. Butterworth high-pass filter, order 3, cutoff frequency 800 Hz

#Equipment#
Fostex FR-2 digital recorder with Sennheiser microphone and Telinga pro 22" parabolic reflector.

title: XC356971 Wood Duck (Aix sponsa)
location: Skidaway Island, Chatham County, GA USA
description: At times, in this particular location of fresh water ponds this species can be quite common.  The pools will dry up in drought periods and the birds are obviously not there.  I have counted as many as 55 individuals in three ponds during wet winters.  They are skittish and notoriously hard to get close to, taking flight very easily.  Two birds seemed undisturbed as I slowed my vehicle to a stop.  I was able to get out and work my way to the water's edge before they took off, which allowed me to get their fading calls, which for all the world sounds like they are in dire straits.
author: Russ Wigh

title: XC316440 Wood Thrush (Hylocichla mustelina)
location: Oxford, Lafayette County, Mississippi
description:
Natural sound. Bird singing from a perch 4m above the ground in a small hackberry tree at the eastern edge of the grounds.  

#Habitat#
29-acre estate centrally located in Oxford, MS consisting of antebellum home surrounded by lawns and adjacent forest. Privet hedges and small thickets divide the grounds into distinct lawn units. Bordered on all sides by mature oak-hickory forest. Forest edge consists of oak spp, hickory spp, red cedar, mulberry, with understory along the edge dominated by privet (Ligustrum sp.). Grounds around the house include isolated trees and manicured hedges. A path from the end of the parking area leads northward ~1 km through the forest to the northern edge of the property abutting the University of Mississippi campus

#Editing#
Edited in Adobe Audition. Butterworth high-pass filter, order 3, cutoff frequency 800 Hz

#Equipment#
Fostex FR-2 digital recorder with Sennheiser microphone and Telinga pro 22" parabolic reflector.
author: J.R. Rigby

title: XC150001 Yellow-bellied Flycatcher (Empidonax flaviventris)
location: Wekiwa Springs State Park, Apopka, Orange, Florida
description: This bird was recorded from a boat along the Wekiva River on March 1, 2013. The habitat is extensive hardwood floodplain swamp. It called repeatedly for quite some time but never showed itself. The call notes sound like a reasonably good fit to the "turee" type call of YBFL to me. However, this species is quite rare in Florida, especially in winter/spring. I'd appreciate thoughts on this one. I recorded this with my iphone 4s and amplified it slightly using Audacity. It is otherwise unedited. You have to forgive the background noise. Someone was digging through a pelican case on the aluminum boat hull and created a lot of noise. I isolated one call note and cleaned it up a bit. I'll upload that recording momentarily.
author: Graham Williams

secondary_labels: ['Empidonax alnorum_Alder Flycatcher', 'Mniotilta varia_Black-and-white Warbler', 'Setophaga ruticilla_American Redstart']
location: Westborough, Worcester, Massachusetts
description: Recording amplified by 5.  Originally I'd paused to record the Alder Flycatcher, since it was close.  As I turned the recorder on, I heard the 'perwee' sound that I've attributed to the Yellow-bellied Flycatcher.  The sound doesn't fit exactly, but seems to be the best match.  The bird in question calls at 0:00.3, 0:04.0, 0:08.0, 0:15.9, and at 0:27.6 seconds.  Bird was not seen.  Note a Least Flycatcher was singing for a few min before and after this recording.  This recording was from the dense understory adjacent to a swampy wooded wetland.  There were alder trees present.  All birds were well back and tucked in the understory.

title: XC212491 Myrtle Warbler (Setophaga coronata)
location: Skidaway Island, Chatham County, GA USA
description: This chip note is regularly heard throughout the wintering season and is the only vocalization until just prior to spring migration when they begin singing.  My observation is that with this and other species overwintering are more vocal earlier in their arrival, and that in the case of (Myrtle) Yellow-rumps they appear to be more social at that time, concentrations thinning out throughout the winter months. The recording was made with a Sound Devices 722 and a Sennheiser ME64 placed under a tree.  I 'spished' a few times to get their attention and they dutifully came in.  The recording has been amplified since the note is weak, and noise reduction was employed.

Grounds around the house include isolated trees and manicured hedges. A path from the end of the parking area leads northward ~1 km through the forest to the northern edge of the property abutting the University of Mississippi campus

Edited in Adobe Audition. Butterworth high-pass filter, order 3, cutoff frequency 100 Hz

Fostex FR-2 digital recorder with Sennheiser microphone and Telinga pro 22" parabolic reflector.

title: XC357422 Yellow-throated Vireo (Vireo flavifrons)
secondary_labels: ['Amazona autumnalis_Red-lored Parrot', 'Manacus vitellinus_Golden-collared Manakin', 'Pitangus sulphuratus_Great Kiskadee', 'Ramphocaenus melanurus_Long-billed Gnatwren', 'Pachysylvia decurtata_Lesser Greenlet', 'Megaceryle torquata_Ringed Kingfisher']
location: Pipeline Road, Soberania NP
description: While not the loudest song in this recording, the song of the Yellow-throated Vireo is the most interesting at this location. The other species sing many times every day here, whereas this vireo (mostly here only during the northern winter) usually vocalizes its burry call and rarely sings its song. Here it does so at 0:06, 0:09, 0:12, 0:14, 0:20, 0:24, 0:30, and 0:43. Wing snaps of Golden-collared Manakin are at 0:20, 0:22, 0:27, 0:28, and 0:57. A Ringed Kingfisher flew overhead starting at 0:50.
background: Red-lored Amazon (Amazona autumnalis); Golden-collared Manakin (Manacus vitellinus); Great Kiskadee (Pitangus sulphuratus); Trilling Gnatwren (Ramphocaenus melanurus); Lesser Greenlet (Hylophilus decurtatus); Ringed Kingfisher (Megaceryle torquata)
